entry.title: How I Built an AI-Powered ABAP Code Reviewer Using Google Gemini and SAP BTP
entry.content:
How I Built an AI-Powered ABAP Code Reviewer Using Google Gemini and SAP BTP

Introduction

Generative AI is rapidly changing software development, and as an SAP ABAP developer, I wanted to understand how these technologies could be applied to solve real problems within the SAP ecosystem.

One activity that every ABAP developer is familiar with is code review. Before code reaches production, it usually goes through peer reviews, ATC checks, or Code Inspector validations. While these tools are excellent at identifying issues, they often don't explain why a particular coding practice is problematic or how it can be improved.

This inspired me to build a simple AI-powered ABAP Code Reviewer using Google Gemini, Python, and SAP Business Application Studio on SAP BTP. The objective wasn't to replace ATC or Code Inspector, but to provide developers with easy-to-understand explanations and practical improvement suggestions.

In this blog, I'd like to share how I built the application, the technologies I used, the challenges I faced, and the lessons I learned during the process.

The Idea

The application is intentionally simple.

A developer pastes an ABAP program into a web page, clicks Review, and receives an AI-generated analysis covering:

  • Performance issues

  • Modern ABAP best practices

  • Code quality improvements

  • Object-Oriented ABAP recommendations

  • Security considerations

  • S/4HANA and Clean Core guidance

  • Overall code quality rating

The primary focus is helping developers understand why an issue exists instead of simply identifying it.

Technology Stack

The project uses the following technologies:

  • Python

  • Flask

  • Google Gemini 2.5 Flash

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript

  • SAP Business Application Studio on SAP BTP

Python and Flask were used to build the backend API, while SAP Business Application Studio provided a convenient cloud-based development environment.

Overall Architecture

The application follows a straightforward request-response flow:

  1. The developer enters ABAP code in the web interface.

  2. The frontend sends the code to a Flask API.

  3. The backend combines the code with a carefully designed system prompt containing SAP coding guidelines.

  4. Google Gemini reviews the code.

  5. The generated review is returned and displayed in the browser.

Although simple, this architecture allowed me to focus on understanding Generative AI rather than building a complex application.

Building the Application

Step 1 – Setting up the environment

I created a Python project in SAP Business Application Studio and installed the required dependencies, including Flask and the Google Gemini SDK.

 

pip install flask   
pip install google-genai

Step 2 – Prompt Engineering

The most important part of the application wasn't the Flask code—it was the prompt.

Instead of asking Gemini to "review this code," I provided structured SAP-specific instructions covering areas such as:

  • Performance optimization

  • Modern ABAP syntax

  • Object-Oriented ABAP

  • Security checks

  • S/4HANA development practices

  • Clean Core recommendations

This significantly improved the consistency and relevance of the generated reviews.

SYSTEM_PROMPT excerpt:

  SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are an expert SAP ABAP Code Reviewer 
  specializing in Clean Core, S/4HANA development standards, 
  and modern ABAP practices.

  Review the provided ABAP code and analyze it across these areas:

  1. PERFORMANCE: SELECT statements, loops, database calls
  2. MODERN ABAP: Use of newer syntax, inline declarations
  3. CODE QUALITY: Naming conventions, modularity, readability
  4. OO ABAP: Proper use of classes, methods, encapsulation
  5. SECURITY: Authority checks, input validation
  6. S/4HANA & CLEAN CORE: Compatibility with cloud deployment

  Provide an Overall Rating out of 10."""

 

Step 3 – Building the Review API

The Flask API exposes a /review endpoint.

When the user submits ABAP code, the API:

  • validates the request,

  • combines the code with the system prompt,

  • sends the request to Google Gemini,

  • returns the generated review as JSON.

Despite being only a few lines of code, this endpoint forms the core of the application.

@app.route("/review", methods=["POST"])
  def review():
      code = request.json.get("code", "")
      if not code.strip():
          return jsonify({"error": "No code provided"}), 400
  
      prompt = f"{SYSTEM_PROMPT}\n\nReview this ABAP code:\n\n{code}"
      response = client.models.generate_content(
          model="gemini-2.5-flash",
          contents=prompt
      )
      return jsonify({"review": response.text})

Step 4 – Creating the User Interface

For the frontend, I kept the interface intentionally simple.

The page contains:

  • a text area for entering ABAP code,

  • a Review button,

  • an output section that displays the AI-generated review.

My objective was to focus on the AI integration rather than frontend complexity.

 

Demo

 

Challenges I Faced

The biggest challenge during development was integrating the latest Google Gemini SDK.

While following online examples, I noticed that many tutorials used the older google.generativeai package, which has since been replaced by the newer google.genai package. Updating the project to the latest SDK and resolving API compatibility issues required some experimentation.

This experience also highlighted how quickly AI libraries evolve and the importance of referring to the latest documentation.

What I Learned

This project taught me much more than simply calling an AI model.

Some of my biggest learnings were:

  • Building Python web applications using Flask.

  • Developing applications within SAP Business Application Studio.

  • Integrating Generative AI into enterprise applications.

  • Understanding how prompt engineering influences AI output.

  • Appreciating how SAP domain knowledge can improve AI-generated recommendations.

Future Improvements

This project is only the first version.

Some enhancements I plan to explore include:

  • Migrating from Flask to FastAPI.

  • Separating AI prompts from application logic.

  • Adding deterministic rule-based checks before invoking the LLM.

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using SAP documentation.

  • GitHub Pull Request integration for automated code reviews.

  • Support for additional SAP development guidelines.

Conclusion

This project showed me that combining SAP expertise with Generative AI can produce practical developer tools.

Rather than replacing existing SAP tools such as ATC or Code Inspector, AI can complement them by explaining findings, suggesting improvements, and helping developers adopt modern development practices more quickly.

If you're an SAP developer interested in Generative AI, I encourage you to start with a small project that solves a real problem you encounter in your daily work. Building something practical is one of the best ways to learn.

The complete source code for this project is available on GitHub:

https://github.com/AryaRanjan3101/sap-ai-code-reviewer

I'd be happy to hear your suggestions or ideas for improving the project.

entry.title: Building and Deploying Your First MCP Server on SAP BTP
entry.content:
1. Understanding MCP

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard that lets an AI model call external tools and read data in a structured way. Think of it like a USB standard for AI — just as USB lets any device plug into any computer, MCP lets any tool plug into any AI model.

 

The Three Primitives

An MCP server can expose three types of capabilities:

 

Primitive

Purpose

Analogy

Tools

Functions the AI can call and execute — like pressing a button

A menu item in a restaurant

Resources

Data the AI can read as context — like a reference document

A reference manual

Prompts

Reusable prompt templates the AI or user can invoke

A saved workflow

In this tutorial we focus on Tools — the most powerful primitive for SAP integration.

 

Architecture

The flow is simple:

 

 

 

 

 

The user types a natural language request. The AI reads the tool descriptions (docstrings), decides which tool to call, the MCP server executes the OData call, and returns the formatted result to the AI — which then replies to the user.

 

2. Prerequisites

 

Before we start, ensure you have the following installed and configured:

 

Requirement

Version

Purpose

Python

3.10+

Runtime for the MCP server

VS Code

Latest

IDE for development and debugging

Node.js

18+

Required for the MCP Inspector browser UI

CF CLI

v8+

Deploy to SAP BTP Cloud Foundry

SAP BTP Account

—

Cloud Foundry environment with a space

Install the VS Code Python extension from the Extensions marketplace (Ctrl+Shift+X → search Python → Install).

 

3. Setting Up VS Code

 

Step 1 — Create the Project Folder

 

Open VS Code and go to File → Open Folder. Create a new folder called my_first_mcp and open it. Your VS Code Explorer should show MY_FIRST_MCP at the top.

 

Step 2 — Open the Terminal

 

Go to Terminal → New Terminal. A terminal panel opens at the bottom of VS Code.

 

Step 3 — Create a Virtual Environment

 

A virtual environment isolates your project's Python packages from the rest of your system — each project has its own clean set of dependencies.

 

python3 -m venv .venv --upgrade-deps

 

Activate it:

 

Mac / Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

Windows:

.venv\Scripts\activate

Your terminal prompt changes to show (.venv) — this confirms the environment is active.

VS Code may prompt 'Do you want to select this environment as the workspace interpreter?' — click Yes. This ensures the debugger uses the correct Python.

 

Step 4 — Install Dependencies

 

pip install "mcp[cli]" httpx

 

This installs two packages:

  • mcp[cli] — FastMCP server and the mcp dev Inspector command
  • httpx — an async HTTP client for making OData calls

Verify the installation:

 

mcp version

You should see the mcp version number printed.

 

4. Building the MCP Server

Create a new file in your project folder called server_trippin.py. This will be our complete MCP server.

 

Step 1 — The Server Skeleton

Every MCP server starts with the same three lines:

 

import httpx

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("TripPin Server")

BASE_URL = "https://services.odata.org/TripPinRESTierService"

FastMCP is the high-level framework that handles the MCP protocol for us. We give the server a name and set the base URL for our OData service.

 

Step 2 — Understanding the Tool Pattern

Every tool follows the same pattern:

 

@mcp.tool()

async def tool_name(parameter: type) -> str:

    """Docstring — the AI reads this to know when to use this tool."""

    # make HTTP call

    # parse response

    # return formatted string

 

Part

What it does

@mcp.tool()

Registers this function as an MCP tool

Function name

Becomes the tool name the AI calls

Parameters + types

Become the tool's input schema automatically

Docstring

The AI reads this to decide when to use the tool

Return value

Sent back to the AI as the tool result

 

Step 3 — The GET Tools (Read Operations)

Let's add our first two tools — listing and fetching people:

 

@mcp.tool()

async def get_people(top: int = 5) -> str:

    """Get a list of people. top = how many to return (default 5)."""

    url = f"{BASE_URL}/People"

    params = {"$format": "json", "$top": top,

              "$select": "UserName,FirstName,LastName,Gender"}

    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:

        response = await client.get(url, params=params)

    people = response.json()["value"]

    lines = []

    for p in people:

        lines.append(f"Username:{p['UserName']:<20} {p['FirstName']} {p['LastName']}")

    return "\n".join(lines)



@mcp.tool()

async def get_person(username: str) -> str:

    """Get details of a single person by username."""

    url = f"{BASE_URL}/People('{username}')"

    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:

        response = await client.get(url, params={"$format": "json"})

    if response.status_code == 404:

        return f"Person '{username}' not found."

    p = response.json()

    return (f"Username  : {p['UserName']}\n"

            f"First Name: {p['FirstName']}\n"

            f"Last Name : {p['LastName']}\n"

            f"Emails    : {', '.join(p.get('Emails', []))}")

Notice we use async/await with httpx.AsyncClient(). This is important — MCP tools should be async so the server can handle multiple requests efficiently.

 

Step 4 — The POST Tool (Create)

 

@mcp.tool()

async def create_person(username: str, first_name: str, last_name: str) -> str:

    """Create a new person in TripPin."""

    url = f"{BASE_URL}/People"

    payload = {

        "UserName": username,

        "FirstName": first_name,

        "LastName": last_name,

        "Emails": [], "AddressInfo": [], "Features": []

    }

    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:

        response = await client.post(

            url, json=payload,

            headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}

        )

    if response.status_code in (200, 201):

        p = response.json()

        return f"Created: {p['UserName']} — {p['FirstName']} {p['LastName']}"

    return f"Failed. HTTP {response.status_code}: {response.text[:200]}"

 

Step 5 — The PATCH Tool (Update)

 

@mcp.tool()

async def update_person(username: str, first_name: str = "", last_name: str = "") -> str:

    """Update an existing person's first or last name."""

    url = f"{BASE_URL}/People('{username}')"

    payload = {}

    if first_name: payload["FirstName"] = first_name

    if last_name:  payload["LastName"]  = last_name

    if not payload: return "Nothing to update."

    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:

        response = await client.patch(

            url, json=payload,

            headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}

        )

    if response.status_code in (200, 204):

        return f"Person '{username}' updated successfully."

    return f"Failed. HTTP {response.status_code}"

 

Step 6 — The DELETE Tool

 

@mcp.tool()

async def delete_person(username: str) -> str:

    """Delete a person by username."""

    url = f"{BASE_URL}/People('{username}')"

    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:

        response = await client.delete(url)

    if response.status_code in (200, 204):

        return f"Person '{username}' deleted successfully."

    return f"Failed. HTTP {response.status_code}"

 

Step 7 — The Entry Point

Add this at the very bottom of server_trippin.py:

 

if __name__ == "__main__":

    import os, asyncio

    transport = os.getenv("MCP_TRANSPORT", "stdio")

    port = int(os.getenv("PORT", 8080))

    if transport == "sse":

        mcp.settings.port = port

        mcp.settings.host = "0.0.0.0"

        asyncio.run(mcp.run_sse_async())

    else:

        asyncio.run(mcp.run_stdio_async())

This block handles both local development (stdio) and BTP deployment (SSE) using an environment variable. When running locally with mcp dev, it uses stdio. When deployed to BTP with MCP_TRANSPORT=sse, it switches to SSE mode.

 

5. Testing Locally with MCP Inspector

MCP Inspector is a browser-based UI that lets you call every tool interactively — without needing Claude Desktop or any AI client. It is the fastest way to test and debug your tools.

 

Step 1 — Run the Server

In the VS Code terminal (with .venv active):

 

mcp dev server_trippin.py

 

You will see output like:

 

Starting MCP inspector...

Proxy server listening on localhost:6277

MCP Inspector is up and running at:

http://localhost:6274/?MCP_PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN=...

 

Open the URL shown in your browser.

 

Step 2 — Connect and Test

 

In the MCP Inspector browser UI:

  • Click Connect to connect to your running server
  • Click the Tools tab — you should see all 5 tools listed
  • Click get_people → enter top=5 → click Run

 enter top=5 → click Run

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

You should see a formatted list of people returned from the TripPin OData service.

If the Inspector cannot connect, check that the terminal shows the server running and that you copied the full URL including the token parameter.

 

Step 3 — Test All CRUD Operations

 

Tool

Test Input

Expected Result

get_people

top=5

List of 5 people with username and name

get_person

username=angelhuffman

Full details of Angel Huffman

create_person

username=testuser, first_name=Test, last_name=User

Confirmation with new user details

update_person

username=testuser, first_name=Updated

Update successful message

delete_person

username=testuser

Deletion successful message

The TripPin service uses session-based URLs. If you get a redirect error, open the TripPin URL in your browser, copy the session ID from the redirected URL (e.g. /TripPinRESTierService/(S(xxxxxxxxxx))/), and update BASE_URL in your server.

 

6. Deploying to SAP BTP Cloud Foundry

Now that our MCP server works locally, let's deploy it to SAP BTP Cloud Foundry so it can be accessed remotely by any MCP-compatible AI client.

 

Step 1 — Create requirements.txt

Create a file called requirements.txt in your project folder:

 

mcp[cli]==1.2.0

httpx

uvicorn

We pin mcp to version 1.2.0 specifically. Later versions (1.5+) include strict host header validation that conflicts with SAP BTP's GoRouter reverse proxy, causing 421 Misdirected Request errors. Version 1.2.0 is stable and works correctly on BTP.

 

Step 2 — Create manifest.yml

Create a file called manifest.yml:

 

applications:

  - name: mcp-trippin-server

    buildpacks:

      - python_buildpack

    memory: 256M

    instances: 1

    command: python server_trippin.py

    env:

      MCP_TRANSPORT: sse

      DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH: "true"

Key settings explained:

  • python_buildpack — tells BTP to use the Python runtime
  • memory: 256M — sufficient for a lightweight MCP server
  • MCP_TRANSPORT: sse — switches our server to SSE mode on BTP
  • DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH — required for the Inspector to connect without token auth

 

Step 3 — Log in to Cloud Foundry

 

cf login -a https://api.cf.<your-region>.hana.ondemand.com

Enter your BTP email and password when prompted, then select your org and space.

 

Step 4 — Deploy

 

cf push mcp-trippin-server -f manifest.yml

 

BTP will:

  • Upload your project files
  • Download the Python buildpack
  • Install all packages from requirements.txt
  • Start the server on port 8080

 

This takes approximately 2-3 minutes. When complete you will see:

 

state     since          cpu    memory

#0   running   2026-07-18   0.2%   45M of 256M

 

Step 5 — Verify Deployment

 

cf apps

You should see your app with status started and 1/1 instances running:

name                  requested state   instances   memory   routes

mcp-trippin-server    started           web:1/1     256M     mcp-trippin-server.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

7. Testing the Deployed Server

With the server live on BTP, let's connect the MCP Inspector to the remote URL.

Step 1 — Run MCP Inspector

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector

Step 2 — Connect to BTP

In the Inspector browser UI:

  • Change the transport dropdown from stdio to SSE
  • Enter your BTP server URL:
https://mcp-trippin-server.cfapps.<your-region>.hana.ondemand.com/sse

Click Connect

You should see the Tools tab appear with all 5 tools listed.

Step 3 — Test a Live Tool Call

Click get_people, enter top=5, and click Run. You should see live data returned from the TripPin OData service through your BTP-hosted MCP server.

You can also monitor your live server logs from the terminal: cf logs mcp-trippin-server — this streams all incoming requests and responses in real time.

 

Checking the BTP Cockpit

You can also verify your deployment in the SAP BTP Cockpit:

  • Log in to cockpit.btp.cloud.sap
  • Navigate to your subaccount → Cloud Foundry → Spaces → your space
  • Click Applications — you will see mcp-trippin-server with status Running
  • Click the app to see memory usage, logs, and environment variables

 

8. Key Lessons Learned

Deploying MCP servers to SAP BTP has some specific considerations worth highlighting:

 

Lesson

Detail

Pin MCP to 1.2.0

MCP 1.5+ has strict host validation incompatible with BTP's GoRouter. Pin to 1.2.0 in requirements.txt.

Use SSE not Streamable HTTP

BTP's GoRouter blocks Streamable HTTP (/mcp endpoint) with 421 errors. SSE (/sse endpoint) works correctly.

Port must be 8080

BTP Cloud Foundry always sets the PORT environment variable to 8080. Read it with int(os.getenv('PORT', 8080)).

Use mcp.settings for config

Set mcp.settings.port and mcp.settings.host before calling run_sse_async() — do not pass them as arguments.

Debug with cf logs

Use cf logs <app-name> --recent to see the last 100 lines, or cf logs <app-name> for live streaming.

Session URLs in TripPin

TripPin redirects to session URLs. If you get redirect errors, update BASE_URL with the session ID from the redirected URL.

 

Conclusion

The Model Context Protocol represents a fundamental shift in how we think about enterprise AI integration. Instead of building complex AI workflows that understand your SAP data model, you simply wrap your existing OData services in a few lines of Python — and any AI model can now interact with your SAP system in natural language.

What we built today is just the beginning. A maintenance engineer can now ask "show me all overdue work orders for plant PL01" instead of navigating through Fiori screens. A planner can say "release order 1000001" instead of executing a transaction. The AI handles the intent — your MCP server handles the execution.

The pattern you learned here scales to any SAP service. The same @mcp.tool() decorator, the same httpx async client, the same OData response parsing — whether you are calling TripPin, Northwind, or your production iSAM Maintenance Foundation service on S/4HANA.

SAP BTP Cloud Foundry gives you a reliable, enterprise-grade hosting platform for your MCP servers — keeping your tools close to your SAP landscape, inside your security boundary, and manageable through standard CF tooling you already know.

We are at an early but exciting moment. MCP is rapidly becoming the standard way AI agents interact with enterprise systems. As SAP developers, we are uniquely positioned to build these bridges — combining decades of SAP domain knowledge with modern AI tooling.

I hope this tutorial gives you the foundation to start building. Try replacing TripPin with one of your own SAP OData services, deploy it to BTP, and connect it to Claude Desktop. The moment your AI calls a real SAP transaction in natural language for the first time is genuinely exciting.

If you have questions, run into issues, or build something interesting — drop a comment below. I would love to see what the SAP community creates with MCP.

Happy building.

#MCP  #ModelContextProtocol  #SAPBTP  #CloudFoundry  #Python  #GenerativeAI  #AIAgents  #SAPDevelopers  #LLM  #OData

entry.title: Explaining the Predictions of an APL Gradient Boosting Model
entry.content:
APL Gradient Boosting from the hana-ml Python package comes with a built-in HTML chart that explains the predictions made by the model. This blog illustrates how to generate such a graph whether your machine learning scenario is a classification or a regression scenario.

 

General Versus Local Explanations

 

In machine learning two different levels of explanations are considered: general and local.

General explanations are available as soon as the predictive model is trained (fit operation). Thanks to them the user can understand what the most important variables are overall.

Local explanations require predictions to be made (predict operation). We then see the contributions of the variables for each individual prediction.

In both cases, general and local, APL uses the SHAP framework (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and presents the results in a pre-canned HTML chart.

 

Training Dataset

 

The two coming examples involve the same dataset census, for the sake of simplicity.

First things first, we connect to HANA Cloud:

from hana_ml import dataframe as hd
conn = hd.ConnectionContext(
    address = 'Host_String', port = 443, 
    user = 'USER_APL', password = 'Password_String', 
    encrypt = 'true', sslValidateCertificate = 'false' )
conn.connection.isconnected()

Then we define the HANA dataframe for the training data:

sql_cmd = 'select * from apl_samples.census order by "id"'
hdf_train = hd.DataFrame(conn, sql_cmd)
print("Number of Rows:", hdf_train.count())
print("Number of Columns:", hdf_train.shape[1])
print("Columns name:", hdf_train.columns)
hdf_train.tail(6).collect()

The order by clause on the table’s primary key permits a repeatable APL model.

 

Regression scenario

 

For our first example, we train an APL Gradient Boosting model with a continuous target.

ID_COLUMN = "id"
CONTINUOUS_TARGET = 'age'
from hana_ml.algorithms.apl.gradient_boosting_regression import GradientBoostingRegressor
rg_model = GradientBoostingRegressor(variable_auto_selection = True)
rg_model.fit(hdf_train, label=CONTINUOUS_TARGET, key=ID_COLUMN)

Once the model is trained, we prepare the HANA dataframe for the inference data:

sql_cmd = 'select * from apl_samples.census order by "id" limit 100'
hdf_inf_rg = hd.DataFrame(conn, sql_cmd).deselect(CONTINUOUS_TARGET)
print("Number of Rows:", hdf_inf_rg.count())
print("Number of Columns:", hdf_inf_rg.shape[1])
print("Columns name:", hdf_inf_rg.columns)

 

The predictions by the APL model are as follows:

rg_model.predict(hdf_inf_rg).head(3).collect()

 

 

 

You can see the explanations in a table format:

df_rg_expl = rg_model.predict(hdf_inf_rg, prediction_type="Explanations")
df_rg_expl.collect().sort_values([ID_COLUMN, "Explanation_Rank"]).head(20)

But the explanations are easier to interpret when plotted in a chart:

rg_model.build_report()
rg_model.generate_notebook_iframe_report()

 

Each variable contribution is expressed in the unit of the target. On top, the Baseline bar is the average of the target: Age. The black bar at the bottom gives the Age prediction. In between are the different variables impacting negatively the target (red bars) or positively (green bars).

To make the output digestible, APL limits the number of bars. If there are more than 10 predictors, APL sums the small positive contributions into a group called “Positive Others”, and the small negative into a second group called “Negative Others”.

You may have noticed, in the pandas dataframe, that the predicted age is an integer value, whereas in the waterfall chart it has decimals. If you want the predicted values with decimals everywhere, insert this code just before the fit operation:

rg_model.set_params(
    variable_storages=   {'age': 'number'},
    variable_value_types={'age': 'continuous'}
)

To share the waterfall chart with your business user, save the report as an HTML file like this:

rg_model.generate_html_report('apl_chart')

 

 

Classification scenario

 

Our second example follows the same steps as in the first example, but we will see at the end that the resulting chart for local explanations is of a different kind.

We train, this time, a binary classification model.

ID_COLUMN = "id"
BINARY_TARGET = 'class'
from hana_ml.algorithms.apl.gradient_boosting_classification import GradientBoostingBinaryClassifier
bc_model = GradientBoostingBinaryClassifier(variable_auto_selection = True)
bc_model.fit(hdf_train, label=BINARY_TARGET, key=ID_COLUMN)

Then we build the inference HANA dataframe.

sql_cmd = 'select * from apl_samples.census order by "id" limit 100'
hdf_inf_bc = hd.DataFrame(conn, sql_cmd).deselect(BINARY_TARGET)
print("Number of Rows:", hdf_inf_bc.count())
print("Number of Columns:", hdf_inf_bc.shape[1])
print("Columns name:", hdf_inf_bc.columns)

 

Now, we can predict the binary class.

bc_model.predict(hdf_inf_bc).head(5).collect()

 

 

 

 

Here are the explanations for each prediction:

df_bc_expl = bc_model.predict(hdf_inf_bc, prediction_type="Explanations")
df_bc_expl.collect().sort_values([ID_COLUMN, "Explanation_Rank"]).head(20)

 

The contribution (last column), in the case of a classification model, is an unbounded value, not easy to understand. That’s where the Strength indicator (second to last column) comes into play:

Strength = Contribution / Sigma
Sigma being the standard deviation of all the contributions.

This normalized indicator, varying roughly between -6 sigma and +6 sigma, estimates for each row the impact that a given variable has on the predicted value. A positive strength means the variable pushes the prediction toward the positive class.

From the strength value, one can obtain a qualitative strength level by defining ranges like the following:

Condition

Strength level

> 3

Strong Positive

> 1

Meaningful Positive

> 0

Weak Positive

≥ -1

Weak Negative

≥ -3

Meaningful Negative

< -3

Strong Negative

 

Last, we generate the chart:

 

 

The same kind of chart is provided by APL if you predict a multi-class target instead of a binary target.

 

To know more about APL

entry.title: Connecting to an On-Premise PostgreSQL Database from a BTP Python Application
entry.content:
Introduction

This blog aims to demonstrate how it is possible to deploy a python application on SAP BTP and connect to a PostgreSQL database located on-premise, using SAP Cloud Connector.

Acknowledgement

This blog heavily draws inspiration from the following blogs by @felixbartler :

  • https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-sap/sap-cloud-foundry-python-and-cloud-connector-tcp/ba-p/13967140
  • https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-sap/proxy-third-party-python-library-traffic-general/ba-p/13557613

In essence, this blog can be seen as an extension to the above blogs, and it tries to showcase one complete practical application, synthesizing the concepts from the above blogs.

The objective - what we are trying to achieve

The situation:

  • We have an existing Postgres database with a few tables in our local, on-premise network
  • We need to create an application on BTP to access the data from this database

The task:

  • Create a python application on SAP BTP
  • Utilize the standard connection mechanism of python to Postgres database, i.e. psycopg2 library, and route the connection via cloud connector, and connect to the on-premise Postgres database.
  • As proof-of-concept (POC), we will select the data from a single table inside a database in Postgres

Architecture Diagram

 

The process flow is as follows:

  1. A PostgreSQL database is installed on-premise.
  2. A cloud connector is installed on the same on-premise network and is connected to an SAP BTP subaccount.
  3. The Postgres is exposed via the cloud connector, over TCP, using a virtual host and virtual port.
  4. A python application is deployed on the same SAP BTP subaccount where the cloud connector is connected.
  5. The python app is based on a FastAPI based application, which uses the psycopg2 library for connection to the database, and calls a local proxy implementation via SocketSwap library, exposed at 127.0.0.1, port 2222
  6. The SocketSwap proxy, in turn, connects to a connection factory that first obtains authentication token from the BTP connectivity service, and then, using the token from the connectivity service, connects to the virtual host and port of the PostgreSQL database through cloud connector.
  7. The python application then uses SELECT query to select data from one of the tables in the database and returns as a JSON, and the JSON is displayed as an output.

This way, the FastAPI app uses the psycopg2 library to connect to the PostgreSQL host located inside the on-premise network.

Environment

This POC was carried out in windows environment. PostgreSQL version used was 16.14, and python version used was 3.13. The BTP platform was my own trial account.

PostgreSQL Installation

For this POC, Postgres is installed in the same system as the cloud connector. There are many tutorials on the internet to discuss the Postgres installation, so I will not detail it out here. The installers / binaries can be downloaded from the following link, and then the instructions in the installers can be followed to set up an Postgres installation:

https://www.postgresql.org/download/

I am using PgAdmin tool for visual monitoring of the database. The database server for this POC, named C3S1, is running on my PC, at port 9000, and it looks as follows over PgAdmin:

 

Inside the server, there is a database “rag_db_c3s7d1”, which houses a set of tables:

 

 

The table named “taxes” holds tax information per country:

 

Our application will try to select the data from this table and display as an output JSON. We will try to execute the following query from our BTP Python application:

SELECT tax_rate FROM taxes WHERE country = ‘USA’

and try to see if the correct tax rate percentage is displayed as the output. If for this query, a tax rate of 8.50 percentage is selected, then the POC will be considered a success.

Cloud Connector Configuration

SAP Cloud Connector is the main component which will provide the on-premise connectivity to the python application on BTP. You can install it by following one of the links below:

  • https://blogs.sap.com/2021/09/05/installation-and-configuration-of-sap-cloud-connector/ - This is referenced in Felix’s Blog
  • https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/sap-cloud-platform-cloud-connector-a-brief-guide-for-beginners/ba-p/13282293 - This is one of the oldest blogs on SAP Cloud Connector, written back in 2015, by Abhradeep Basu , one of the best integration architects I have had the pleasure of working with.

Once the cloud connector is installed and configured, the PostgreSQL database will need to be exposed through it. This is achieved by exposing the host and port of the Postgres DB server as a TCP connection in the cloud connector, Cloud-to-On-premise configuration.

Navigate to the “Cloud-to-On-Premise” section of the cloud connector:

 

Click “Add”:

 

Choose system type as “Non-SAP System” and click “Next”:

 

Choose protocol as “TCP” and click "Next”:

 

Choose the internal host and port, where the Postgres DB is running, and click “Next”.

For our POC, the cloud connector and the Postgres database are running on the same system, hence we choose localhost as the internal host, and the database port is 9000, as mentioned above. You have to adjust these details as per your setup:

 

In the following screen, choose the virtual host and port (the name by which the applications in BTP subaccount will know this database), and click “Next”:

 

Description is optional, we kept it blank. Choose “Next”:

 

Choose “Finish” on the last screen:

 

An entry appears in the cloud connector table. If the connectivity status shows “Unchecked”, then you can choose the “Check Availability” button to check for the connection from the cloud connector to the Postgres host:

 

If the connection works, then the “Check Result” column will turn green:

 

Connectivity Service Configuration

The connectivity service is important in the context of this POC because it will enable the cloud connector connection programmatically from the BTP python application.

To enable a connectivity service instance, we need to go to the subaccount (“trial” in the case of this POC), and navigate to “Instances and Subscriptions”:

 

Click on “Create”:

 

Choose the “Service Name” as “Connectivity Service”, provide a name for the service instance,  and choose “Next”:

 

Keep the parameters blank and choose “Next”:

 

Review and click “Create” in the next screen:

 

The service instance will be created:

 

Now we need to create a service key for the instance. The details from this service key will be utilized at runtime by the python application, to generate an authentication token and programmatically authorize the call to cloud connector tunnel socket.

Click on the three dots beside the connectivity service instance and choose “Create Service Key”:

 

Provide a name of the service key, keep the parameters blank, and click on “Create”:

 

The service key is created:

 

Note the following details from the JSON embedded inside the service key:

  • clientid
  • clientsecret
  • token_service_url
  • onpremise_proxy_host
  • onpremise_socks5_proxy_port

These details will be required for the python application development.

Cloud Foundry CLI Tool Installation and Initialization

The BTP Cloud Foundry command line interface (CLI) tool will help us to deploy the python application on BTP.

The cloud foundry CLI can be downloaded from the following link:

https://github.com/cloudfoundry/cli#downloads

Once you execute the installer, the installer asks for the path to the installation folder, as shown below:

 

And then the installation takes place.

After installation, we will have to set up the API endpoint as a one-time setup. For that, use the “cf api” command as shown below:

 

We will obtain the API URL from your subaccount details in BTP cockpit:

 

Once the API endpoint is set, we will need to use the “cf login” command to login to the cloud foundry account. You will have to provide your account email and password to login, and the cli tool will connect with those credentials:

 

Now we are ready for development in python and deploying it to BTP.

Python Development

The python file structure inside the root directory looks as follows:

python-onpremdbaccess/          # Root directory
├── connect_config.py           # Connection Configuration
├── db_conn_cloud_connector.py  # Connection factory for Cloud Connector
├── manifest.yaml               # Descriptor file for BTP App
├── requirements.txt            # Contains dependencies
├── runtime.txt                 # Contains Python Runtime version info
├── server.py                   # Main FastAPI entry point
└── README.md                   # This file

The various files perform the following activity:

  • server.py: Main API entry point for the on-premise app; builds the FastAPI service and connects through a proxy socket.
  • connect_config.py: Stores the PostgreSQL database credentials and SAP BTP connectivity settings used for token generation and proxy access.
  • db_conn_cloud_connector.py: Creates the SAP Cloud Connector socket that connects to the on-premise database via the configured proxy.
  • manifest.yaml: Holds the deployment details for the BTP application.
  • requirements.txt: Holds the details of the dependencies to be installed for the application to properly work.
  • runtime.txt: Holds the python runtime version information.

Codes for the files are given below.

connect_config.py

import requests
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)

# --- Database configuration -------------------------------------------------
DB_CONFIG = {
    "host": "<your_db_virtual_host_from_cloud_connector>",
    "port": "<your_db_virtual_port_from_cloud_connector>",
    "dbname": "<your_db_name>",
    "user": "<your_db_user>",
    "password": "<your_db_password>",
}

location_id = "<your_cloud_connector_location_id>"  # Adjust to match your Cloud Connector location
client_id = "<your_connectivity_service_client_id>"  # Adjust to match your Connectivity Service client ID
client_secret = "<your_connectivity_service_client_secret>"  # Adjust to match your Connectivity Service client secret
tenant_url = "<your_sap_btp_tenant_url>"  # Adjust to match your SAP BTP tenant URL
token_service_url = "<your_sap_btp_tenant_token_service_url>" # Adjust to match your SAP BTP tenant token service URL
onpremise_proxy_host = "<your_on_premise_proxy_host>"  # Adjust to match your on-premise proxy host
onpremise_proxy_port = "<your_on_premise_proxy_port>"  # Adjust to match your on-premise proxy port
onpremise_socks5_proxy_port = "<your_on_premise_SOCKS5_proxy_port>"  # Adjust to match your on-premise SOCKS5 proxy port

def get_connectivity_service_token():
    """
    Fetches an OAuth token from the SAP Connectivity Service.
    """
    logging.info("Connectivity Service Token Function Called")
    response = requests.post(
        url=token_service_url,
        params={"grant_type": "client_credentials"},
        auth=(client_id, client_secret)
    )

    if response.status_code != 200:
        print(f"Error: {response.status_code} - {response.text}")
        exit(-1)
    logging.info("Connectivity Service Request Status 200")
    logging.debug(f"Access Token: {response.json().get('access_token')}")   # Should be avoided, for test only
    return response.json().get("access_token")

As can be seen from the code above, the file houses the various connection parameters, and provides a function for obtaining the OAuth token from the connectivity service.

Important: the connectivity service token URL from the service key of the connectivity service ends with the suffix ondemand.com. However, the actual call to the token service resides at /oauth/token endpoint under it. So when you are setting the token URL in the file above, make sure to suffix the URL from the connectivity service with /oauth/token, so that it looks something similar to the below URL:

token_service_url = "https://xyztrial.authentication.us10.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token"

 

db_conn_cloud_connector.py

from sapcloudconnectorpythonsocket import CloudConnectorSocket
from connect_config import DB_CONFIG, get_connectivity_service_token, location_id, onpremise_proxy_host, onpremise_socks5_proxy_port
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)

def conn_factory():
    logging.info("Inside Connection Factory Function")

    # Get an OAuth token from the Connectivity Service
    token = get_connectivity_service_token()

    logging.info("After Token, Inside Connection Factory Function")
    
    cc_socket = CloudConnectorSocket()
    logging.info("CC Socket Created, Inside Connection Factory Function")
    logging.info(f"Host: {DB_CONFIG['host']}, Port: {DB_CONFIG['port']}, Proxy Host: {onpremise_proxy_host}, Proxy Port: {onpremise_socks5_proxy_port}, Location ID: {location_id}")
    cc_socket.connect(
            dest_host=DB_CONFIG["host"], 
            dest_port=int(DB_CONFIG["port"]), 
            proxy_host=onpremise_proxy_host, 
            proxy_port=int(onpremise_socks5_proxy_port), 
            token=token,
            location_id=location_id
        )
    logging.info("CC Socket Connected, Inside Connection Factory Function")
    return cc_socket

As can be seen, the above code imports the connectivity details from the  connect_config.py and then inside the conn_factory method, gets an OAuth token from the connectivity service and then opens a cloud connector socket via the proxy host and SOCKS5 proxy port of the connectivity service, and connects to the virtual host and port of the database server located on-premise.

server.py

import os
from cfenv import AppEnv
import psycopg2
import uvicorn

from sap import xssec
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from fastapi import FastAPI, APIRouter, HTTPException
from typing import Optional, List

from sapcloudconnectorpythonsocket import CloudConnectorSocket
from SocketSwap import SocketSwapContext
from db_conn_cloud_connector import conn_factory
from connect_config import DB_CONFIG
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)

app = FastAPI(
    title="DB Query API",
    description="REST API for querying PostGreSql DB",
    version="1.0.0"
)
env = AppEnv()

port = int(os.environ.get('PORT', 3000))

# The single table/column this app is allowed to query.
# Hard-coding these (rather than accepting them from a request) avoids SQL
# injection, since table/column names can't be parameterized like values can.
TABLE_NAME = "taxes"
COLUMN_NAME = "tax_rate"

class QueryResponse(BaseModel):
    value: str 


def get_connection():
    """
    This function demos how to easily setup the local proxy using the SocketSwapContext-Manager.
    It exposes a local proxy on the localhost 127.0.0.1 on port 2222
    The connection factory is provided to handle the creation of a socket to the remote target
    """
    logging.info("Inside Get Connection Function")
    with SocketSwapContext(conn_factory, [], "127.0.0.1", 2222):
        conn = psycopg2.connect(
            host="127.0.0.1",
            database=DB_CONFIG["dbname"],
            user=DB_CONFIG["user"],
            password=DB_CONFIG["password"],
            port=2222
        )
    logging.info("SocketSwap Call Completed, Inside Get Connection Function")
    return conn


@app.get("/", response_model=QueryResponse)
def hello():


    query = f"SELECT {COLUMN_NAME} FROM {TABLE_NAME} WHERE country = 'USA' LIMIT 1;"
 
    try:
        
        conn = get_connection()
        try:
            logging.info("Executing query")
            with conn.cursor() as cur:
                cur.execute(query)
                rows = cur.fetchall()
            logging.info("Query Execution Completed")
        finally:
            conn.close()
    except psycopg2.Error as e:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"Database error: {e}")
 
    logging.info("Looping through rows to get value")
    for row in rows:
        value = str(row[0])
        return QueryResponse(value=value)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    uvicorn.run(app, host='0.0.0.0', port=port)

As can be seen from above, the code does the following:

  • It exposes a FastAPI GET entry point
  • Inside the GET method, it formulates a SELECT query, referring to a table and column. The SELECT query is hard-coded for this POC to one country code and a single row; please feel free to adjust the code as per your use case.
  • Then the method calls a get_connection function.
  • The get_connection function uses SocketSwapContext method from SocketSwap package, to swap the connection to 127.0.0.1 host and port 2222 via the psycopg2 library for connection to Postgres, to a connection socket provided by the conn_factory method. Please recall that the conn_factory method was defined in the previously explained db_conn_cloud_connector.py file, and it opened a connectivity to the DB virtual host and port via cloud connector. So, this mechanism fuses the concept of TCP connectivity to the database host via cloud connector, and the connectivity to a specific database inside the host, using a username and password, via the psycopg2 library.
  • Once the connection is opened, the code executes the SELECT query and retrieves the data set.
  • Then it closes the connection, and loops over the retrieved rows and sends the first retrieved row as JSON response via a pydantic model.

requirements.txt

# Runtime dependencies for the on-premise DB access app
cfenv>=0.5.3,<1.0.0
fastapi>=0.115.0,<1.0.0
uvicorn[standard]>=0.30.0,<1.0.0
pydantic>=2.7.0,<3.0.0
psycopg2-binary>=2.9.0,<3.0.0
requests>=2.31.0,<3.0.0
sap-xssec>=4.0.0,<5.0.0
sapcloudconnectorpythonsocket>=0.1.0
SocketSwap>=0.1.0
PySocks>=1.7.0,<2.0.0

As described, this file details out the dependencies.

runtime.txt

python-3.13.x

As described, it defines the runtime for deployment of the application.

manifest.yaml

---
applications:
- name: zmyapp
  random-route: true
  path: .
  memory: 256M
  buildpacks:
    - python_buildpack
  command: python -m uvicorn server:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port $PORT

The important elements of the descriptor serve the following purpose:

  • The "name" attribute provides a name to the application.
  • The "random-route: true" attribute generates a random URL for the application.
  • The "command" attribute tells the runtime about which command to run to execute the application. As this is a FastAPI application, so the command uvicorn is used here.

Deployment and Testing

Using a command prompt, navigate to the root directory of your application (python-onpremdbaccess in our POC), and execute the following command (note: you have to be logged in via cf login):

cf push

You will observe a final message similar to the following:

Copy the URL shown in the "routes" section of the command prompt. Open a browser and hit the URL:

If your cloud connector is up and your DB is reachable through cloud connector, then you will see an output on the browser, similar to the following:

You can also check the logs by running the following command:

cf logs <your_app_name> --recent

If you have logging enabled at various points (similar to the code snippets given above), you will be able to observe the logs in the output of the above command:

This proves that the application was able to connect to the on-premise database via cloud connector, using psycopg2 library.

Future Enhancements

This proof-of-concept (POC) showcases an end-to-end scenario for connecting from a BTP based python application to an on-premise Postgres database. While this works as a POC, the following enhancements should be considered for an actual productive application:

  • Security – The current POC is not secured by authentication. It should be secured by validating authentication credentials.
  • Dynamic handling of SQL – In the current implementation, the SQL queries to Postgres are pointing to a single table and catering to a single query, located inside the python source file. For more dynamic operations, the query handling should be wrapped around. Also, SQL injection should be prevented, as the final query delivered to the DB is a raw SQL query.
  • User Interface (UI) Development – The python application just prints the output JSON on the browser. A real application will have a proper UI for handling user interaction, which was beyond the scope of the POC, but should be an integral part of a productive application.

Thank you for reading!

entry.title: Beyond SAP Snowflake ML: Calling SAP HANA Cloud ML and RPT-1.5 via External Access Integration (EAI)
entry.content:
SAP Snowflake has been available in the SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) as a Solution Extension for a few months now. In the first post of this series, we built our first ML model natively, using Snowflake's own ML capabilities together with Cortex AI. But what if we want to go beyond that and also leverage SAP's existing AI offerings, such as SAP HANA Cloud's ML capabilities (PAL/APL) and the RPT-1.5 model from Generative AI Hub — all from the same Snowflake Notebook? That's exactly what we'll set up in this hands-on tutorial.

Here we'll wire up an External Access Integration (EAI) so a Snowflake Notebook can securely call two SAP services over the network:

  1. SAP HANA Cloud - connect and run SQL / ML (PAL/APL) remotely.
  2. SAP-RPT-1.5 via Generative AI Hub - the relational foundation model for tabular prediction.

Everything stays governed: credentials live in Snowflake secrets (encrypted at rest), egress is locked down to named hosts via network rules, and access is granted to a single role.

Table of contents

  • Architecture: how External Access Integration (EAI) fits
  • Prerequisites
  • Understanding the building blocks
  • Step 1 - Run the setup SQL
  • Step 2 - Attach the integration & secrets to the notebook
  • Step 3 - Verify from the notebook
  • Step 4 - Connect to SAP HANA Cloud
  • Step 5 - Call the Generative AI Hub
  • Step 6 - Predict with SAP RPT-1.5
  • Troubleshooting
  • Conclusion & Next Steps

Architecture: how External Access Integration (EAI) fits

By default, code running in SAP Snowflake cannot make arbitrary outbound network calls - that's a good security default. An External Access Integration is the account-level object that selectively opens that door. It binds together two kinds of schema-level objects:

  • Network rules - an allowlist of exact host:port destinations for egress.
  • Secrets - encrypted credentials your code reads at runtime.

Once the integration is attached to a notebook's connected service, the notebook can reach the allowed hosts and read the allowed secrets - nothing more.

Prerequisites

  • Access to SAP Business Data Cloud with the Snowflake Solution Extension enabled.
  • The ACCOUNTADMIN role in Snowflake (to create the integration, network rules and secrets).
  • An SAP AI Core service key with a deployed LLM and RPT-1.5 model.
  • SAP HANA Cloud credentials - host, port, user, password.
  • Basic familiarity with SQL and Python.
⚠️Security first. The setup script stores real credentials. Keep the filled-in copy local, never commit it, and rotate the AI Core client secret and HANA password if they are ever exposed. In this blog every credential is shown as a <PLACEHOLDER>.

Understanding the building blocks

Three Snowflake objects work together:

ObjectScopePurpose
NETWORK RULESchemaAllowlist of host:port egress destinations (no wildcards - hosts are matched literally).
SECRETSchemaCredential encrypted at rest. Not even ACCOUNTADMIN can SELECT it; code reads it via the secrets API.
EXTERNAL ACCESS INTEGRATIONAccountBinds the rules + secrets and is attached to a notebook's connected service.

 

💡Network rules and secrets are schema-level, so they need a home. We use a dedicated SAP_INTEGRATION.CONFIG schema to keep them tidy - but your notebook can still run in any database.

Step 1 - Run the setup SQL

Run the following as ACCOUNTADMIN. Here are the key parts.

1a. Create a home for the objects

USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS SAP_INTEGRATION;
CREATE SCHEMA   IF NOT EXISTS SAP_INTEGRATION.CONFIG;
USE DATABASE SAP_INTEGRATION;
USE SCHEMA   CONFIG;

1b. Network rules (egress allowlist)

CREATE OR REPLACE NETWORK RULE aicore_network_rule
  MODE = EGRESS
  TYPE = HOST_PORT
  VALUE_LIST = (
    '<AICORE_AUTH_HOST>',   -- OAuth token server
    '<AICORE_API_HOST>',    -- AI API endpoint
    'ml.hana.ondemand.com'   -- inference deployment domain
  );

CREATE OR REPLACE NETWORK RULE hana_network_rule
  MODE = EGRESS
  TYPE = HOST_PORT
  VALUE_LIST = ( '<HANA_HOST>:443' );
💡Get the host values straight from your AI Core service key: the auth host is the host part of url, and the API host is the host part of serviceurls.AI_API_URL.

1c. Secrets (encrypted at rest)

CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET aicore_secret
  TYPE = GENERIC_STRING
  SECRET_STRING = '{
  "serviceurls": { "AI_API_URL": "<AI_API_URL>" },
  "clientid": "<CLIENT_ID>",
  "clientsecret": "<CLIENT_SECRET>",
  "url": "<AUTH_URL>"
}';

CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET hana_secret
  TYPE = GENERIC_STRING
  SECRET_STRING = '{
  "address": "<HANA_HOST>",
  "port": 443,
  "user": "<HANA_USER>",
  "password": "<HANA_PASSWORD>"
}';

1d. Bind everything into one integration

CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL ACCESS INTEGRATION sap_external_access_integration
  ALLOWED_NETWORK_RULES          = (aicore_network_rule, hana_network_rule)
  ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATION_SECRETS = (aicore_secret, hana_secret)
  ENABLED = TRUE;

1e. Grant to a role

CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS DATA_SCIENTIST;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE SAP_INTEGRATION       TO ROLE DATA_SCIENTIST;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA   SAP_INTEGRATION.CONFIG TO ROLE DATA_SCIENTIST;
GRANT USAGE ON INTEGRATION sap_external_access_integration TO ROLE DATA_SCIENTIST;
GRANT READ  ON SECRET aicore_secret TO ROLE DATA_SCIENTIST;
GRANT READ  ON SECRET hana_secret   TO ROLE DATA_SCIENTIST;

You can also run all of the SQL snippets together in a single execution.

 

 

Step 2 - Attach the integration & secrets to the notebook

Create a Snowflake Notebook (Projects → Workspaces → + Notebook) and switch its role to DATA_SCIENTIST (make sure to add the newly created role to your user before). Then open the notebook's connected service settings and, under External access, enable sap_external_access_integration and attach both secrets (aicore_secret, hana_secret).

 

 

Step 3 - Verify from the notebook

A quick sanity check that the role is right and the objects are visible, then load the secrets at runtime:

SELECT CURRENT_ROLE();
SHOW EXTERNAL ACCESS INTEGRATIONS LIKE 'sap_external_access_integration';
SHOW NETWORK RULES IN SCHEMA SAP_INTEGRATION.CONFIG;

In a SQL cell of a Snowflake Notebook, only the last statement's result is displayed. To see results from all three, you need to put each statement in its own cell.


Next, we verify that the Snowflake Notebook can access the secrets created in the previous step. The secret values are retrieved securely at runtime and parsed as JSON. To avoid exposing sensitive information, we only print non-sensitive connection details such as the AI API URL and the SAP HANA Cloud host.

import json
from snowflake.snowpark.secrets import get_generic_secret_string

aicore_cfg = json.loads(get_generic_secret_string('sap_integration/config/aicore_secret'))
hana_cfg   = json.loads(get_generic_secret_string('sap_integration/config/hana_secret'))
print("AI API URL:", aicore_cfg["serviceurls"]["AI_API_URL"])
print("HANA host :", hana_cfg["address"])
💡The secret path is database/schema/secret_name (case-insensitive). Secrets are read into memory only - nothing is printed to the cell output.

 

Step 4 - Connect to SAP HANA Cloud

Before connecting to SAP HANA Cloud, we need to install the hana-ml python package with a dedicated cell.

%pip install hana-ml

With the credentials in hand, we can now open a hana-ml connection and confirm the version:

import hana_ml.dataframe as dataframe

conn = dataframe.ConnectionContext(
    address=hana_cfg["address"],
    port=hana_cfg["port"],
    user=hana_cfg["user"],
    password=hana_cfg["password"],
)
print("Connected:", conn.connection.isconnected())
print("HANA version:", conn.hana_version())
💡If HANA Cloud filters inbound traffic by IP, print the notebook's egress IP first (requests.get('https://api.ipify.org').text) and add it to the HANA Cloud allowlist. Tip: Snowflake's AI copilot (CoCo) can generate this snippet for you.

 

 

Step 5 - Call the Generative AI Hub

Again, before connecting to the Generative AI Hub, we need to install the sap-ai-sdk-gen python package with a dedicated cell.

%pip install sap-ai-sdk-gen

The sap-ai-sdk-gen python package reads AICORE_* environment variables. Map them from the secret, then prompt a deployed model:

import os
os.environ["AICORE_AUTH_URL"]       = aicore_cfg["url"]
os.environ["AICORE_CLIENT_ID"]      = aicore_cfg["clientid"]
os.environ["AICORE_CLIENT_SECRET"]  = aicore_cfg["clientsecret"]
os.environ["AICORE_BASE_URL"]       = aicore_cfg["serviceurls"]["AI_API_URL"]
os.environ["AICORE_RESOURCE_GROUP"] = "default"

from gen_ai_hub.proxy.native.openai import responses
response = responses.create(
    model="gpt-5",
    instructions="You are a helpful assistant.",
    input="What is the capital of France?",
)
print(response.output_text)

 

Step 6 - Predict with SAP RPT-1.5

RPT-1.5 is SAP's relational foundation model for tabular data. We call its predict endpoint directly with an OAuth token. First, resolve the host so you can confirm it's covered by the network rule:

from urllib.parse import urlparse
DEPLOYMENT_ID = "<YOUR_DEPLOYMENT_ID>"
API_URL = f'{aicore_cfg["serviceurls"]["AI_API_URL"]}/v2/inference/deployments/{DEPLOYMENT_ID}/predict'
print("Predict host:", urlparse(API_URL).hostname)

Then set up a payload which you can later on change for your own specific use case.

payload = {
    "index_column": "id",
    "prediction_config": {
        "target_columns": [
            {
                "name": "category",
                "prediction_placeholder": "?",
                "task_type": "classification",
                "top_k": 1,
            }
        ],
        "explanations": {"top_column_scores": 4, "top_relevant_context_rows": 3},
    },
    "parse_data_types": "true",
    "data_schema": {
        "id": {"dtype": "numeric"},
        "product": {"dtype": "string"},
        "price": {"dtype": "numeric"},
        "category": {"dtype": "string"},
        "stock": {"dtype": "numeric"},
        "production_date": {"dtype": "date"},
    },
    "rows": [
        {"id": 1, "product": "Laptop", "price": 899, "category": "Electronics", "stock": "150", "production_date": "2024-01-15"},
        {"id": 2, "product": "Mouse", "price": 25, "category": "Accessories", "stock": "500", "production_date": "2024-02-20"},
        {"id": 3, "product": "Keyboard", "price": 75, "category": "Accessories", "stock": "320", "production_date": "2024-03-10"},
        {"id": 4, "product": "Monitor", "price": 350, "category": "?", "stock": "200", "production_date": "2024-03-25"},
    ],
}

And lastly, fetch a token and send the tabular payload (predicting the missing category for the last row):

import requests
def get_access_token():
    data = {"grant_type": "client_credentials",
            "client_id": aicore_cfg["clientid"],
            "client_secret": aicore_cfg["clientsecret"]}
    r = requests.post(aicore_cfg["url"] + "/oauth/token", data=data,
                      headers={"Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"})
    return r.json()["access_token"]

token = get_access_token()
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}", "AI-Resource-Group": "default"}
result = requests.post(API_URL, headers=headers, json=payload).json()
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

 

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely cause & fix
Egress / network errorTarget host not in a network rule - add it and re-run the CREATE OR REPLACE NETWORK RULE.
Secret not foundWrong role, secret not attached to the connected service, or wrong db/schema/name path.
401 / OAuth errorClient id/secret expired - rotate the AI Core service key and update aicore_secret.
HANA connection refusedAdd the notebook's egress IP to the HANA Cloud allowlist.

Conclusion & Next Steps

With a single External Access Integration we've securely reached two SAP services - SAP HANA Cloud and Generative AI Hub including RPT-1.5 - from a governed SAP Snowflake notebook. Credentials stayed encrypted, egress stayed locked down, and access was scoped to one role.

From here you can combine these capabilities: pull features from HANA Cloud, enrich them with an LLM, score them with RPT-1.5, and write results back into the SAP landscape.

What's coming next in this series

  • Building Streamlit apps directly in SAP Snowflake.
  • From SAP-managed to custom-managed Data Products - and sharing them back.

Connect with me on LinkedIn to get notified when the next post goes live. Now it's your turn - which SAP AI service would you wire up first? Happy building! 🦾

entry.title: Reading ABAP source code from a BTP ABAP Environment trial with a headless Python script
entry.content:
Introduction

I use ADT in Eclipse to read ABAP code. But recently I needed to read a class's source without Eclipse from a Python script to feed it into a small tool I was building. So a bit of Python can pull the same source, no Eclipse, no browser login.

The reading part was easy. The authentication? That's where I got stuck longer than I'd like to admit  on the BTP ABAP Environment trial. So here's what finally worked, so you don't lose the same evening I did.

This post covers the OAuth flow that works, plus the endpoints for reading a class, interface, include, and function module.

What we'll build

readabapcode/
├── abap_session.py      # OAuth token + one authenticated GET
├── check_connection.py  # prove the pipe works
├── read_abap.py         # CLI: read a class / interface/ include/ FM
└── .env

Prerequisites

A BTP ABAP Environment trial with a developer user (your Eclipse ADT login), Python 3.9+, and two libraries: requests and python-dotenv.

The OAuth grant that actually reads source

Eclipse logs in via a browser; a script can't. Every BTP ABAP system sits behind an XSUAA OAuth instance, and there are two grants you might try. On the trial, only one actually reads source — the detail that cost me the most time:

Grant Token issued? Reading a class
GrantToken issued?Reading a class
client_credentials ✔️ 200❌401 — an HTML logon-failed page ("Anmeldung fehlgeschlagen")
password ✔️ 200✔️source code returned

Both return a token; the difference is whose identity it carries. client_credentials is the OAuth client with no ABAP user behind it, so ADT rejects the read. The password grant sends your own developer username and password (client id/secret as basic auth), and XSUAA issues a token carrying your identity and authorizations — which ADT accepts. No Communication Arrangement needed.

data = {"grant_type": "password", "username": self._user, "password": self._password}
resp = requests.post(
f"{self.oauth_url}/oauth/token",
data=data,
auth=(self.client_id, self.client_secret), # client id/secret as basic auth
timeout=30,
)
token = resp.json()["access_token"]

Every ADT call is then a GET with Authorization: Bearer <token>.

(I only tested the trial on a productive system, whether client_credentials works depends on the communication-user setup. Corrections welcome.)

Create a service key

BTP cockpit → your subaccount → Instances and Subscriptions → open the ABAP environment instance → Service Keys → Create.

From the key, note four values — the root url (→ ABAP_HOST), and under uaa: url (→ OAUTH_URL), clientid (→ CLIENT_ID), and clientsecret (→ CLIENT_SECRET).

Project setup

Create a venv, pip install requests python-dotenv, and a .env (add it to .gitignore so secrets never get committed):

python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install requests python-dotenv

 

ABAP_HOST=https://your-subdomain.abap.us10.hana.ondemand.com
OAUTH_URL=https://your-subdomain.authentication.us10.hana.ondemand.com
CLIENT_ID=your_client_id
CLIENT_SECRET=your_client_secret
SAP_CLIENT=100
# --- Your developer login (OAuth password grant) -------------------------
ABAP_USERNAME=your_btp_username
ABAP_PASSWORD=your_btp_password

The project files

The repo is small — four files:

  • abap_session.py — the core. Reads the .env, gets an access token via the password grant (cached, and refreshed a minute before expiry so reading many objects only authenticates once), and exposes one get() method that runs an authenticated ADT call. It also normalises ADT's CRLF line endings to LF  otherwise, on Windows, you get a blank line between every line of source.
  • check_connection.py — a quick sanity check. It hits the ADT core discovery document (/sap/bc/adt/core/discovery), a cheap endpoint that always exists, so you can prove the connection works before chasing a typo in an object name.
  • read_abap.py — a small CLI over abap_session. You pass an object type and name; it builds the right ADT URL and prints (or saves) the source.
  • .env — your connection details.

Check connection:

python check_connection.py

Reading the source

Reading source is a single GET; only the URL path changes per object type. All four are working in the project:

Object ADT path
Class/sap/bc/adt/oo/classes/{name}/source/main
Interface/sap/bc/adt/oo/interfaces/{name}/source/main
Include/sap/bc/adt/programs/includes/{name}/source/main
Function module/sap/bc/adt/functions/groups/{group}/fmodules/{name}/source/main
python read_abap.py fm z_sum_test_x Z_MJ_TEST
python read_abap.py include LZ_MJ_TESTU01 
python read_abap.py class ZCL_POC_TRAVEL_DATA_REVIEW
python read_abap.py interface IF_ABAP_C_READER

Conclusion

Because ADT is a plain REST API, you're never locked into Eclipse. Once you pick the right OAuth grant — the password grant, so the token carries your developer identity — reading any repository object is a single GET against a predictable URL. From there you can loop over a list of objects, commit them to git for versioning outside transports, or feed the source straight into another tool.

The complete source code for this project is available on GitHub: 

 https://github.com/m2ksap-source/readabapcode 

 

Corrections and better ideas welcome in the comments.

entry.title: Migrating SAP PowerDesigner Object Codes to erwin Data Modeler
entry.content:
Introduction

Migrating a data model between different modeling tools is not only about transferring entities, attributes, and relationships. Preserving source-model traceability can be equally important.

During a migration from SAP PowerDesigner to erwin Data Modeler, the original object codes defined in the source model may need to remain available after migration. Depending on the model type, these codes may originate from a Physical Data Model (PDM), Logical Data Model (LDM), or Conceptual Data Model (CDM).

This blog presents a Python-based approach to extract object codes from a PowerDesigner model and associate them with the corresponding objects in an erwin XML export.

The source object code is stored in the erwin object's Notes as a structured provenance entry:

[Object_code] SMPL_ACQSTN

The important point is that this does not replace existing information in erwin. The code is added as a separate note event, allowing previously migrated comments or notes to remain intact.

1. Migration Approach

The overall process is:

PowerDesigner Model
(PDM / LDM / CDM)
        │
        ▼
Extract Object Codes
        │
        ▼
Match with erwin Objects
        │
        ▼
Add Object Code to erwin Notes
        │
        ▼
Preprocessed erwin XML

The approach can be applied to different PowerDesigner model objects depending on the migration scenario. The generated note follows a simple convention:

[Object_code] <PowerDesigner Object Code>

For example:
[Object_code] SMPL_ACQSTN

This prefix makes the generated provenance information distinguishable from normal documentation or comments.

2. The Traceability Problem

Consider a PowerDesigner object with:

Name: Sample Acquisition
Code: SMPL_ACQSTN

After migration, the corresponding erwin object may contain the name and physical name, but the original PowerDesigner object code may no longer be readily available.

This creates a traceability challenge.

After migration, we may want to answer questions such as:

  • What was the original PowerDesigner object code?
  • Which source object corresponds to this erwin object?
  • Can the migrated object be traced back to the source model?
  • Can the source code be retained without modifying existing documentation?

Instead of introducing a completely separate mapping repository, the approach stores the source object code directly in the corresponding erwin object's Notes.

3. Source-to-Target Concept

The basic concept is:

PowerDesigner Object
        │
        │ Object Code
        ▼
erwin Object Note

For example: 

PowerDesigner
Name: Sample Acquisition
Code: SMPL_ACQSTN

        ↓

erwin Notes
[Object_code] SMPL_ACQSTN

The same concept can be applied to objects originating from a PDM, LDM, or CDM, provided the corresponding source and target objects can be identified.

4. Why Use erwin Notes?

One option would be to modify an existing erwin property to hold the source object code.

However, this can introduce several problems:

  • an existing value could be overwritten;
  • information already migrated from PowerDesigner could be lost;
  • the target model's original information could be altered;
  • repeated migration runs could become difficult to control.

The Notes structure provides a convenient location for maintaining this additional provenance information.

The solution therefore treats the object code as a provenance event, rather than as a replacement for an existing property.

For example: 

Note #1
[Existing migrated comment]

Note #2
[Object_code] SMPL_ACQSTN

If another migration step has already created several notes, the object code becomes the next note instead of replacing them.

5. Understanding the erwin Note Structure

The erwin XML export represents notes using a structure similar to:

<Note_List_Array>
    <Note_List HandleNonPrintableChar="Y" index="0">
        ...
    </Note_List>
</Note_List_Array>

The Note List is associated with the relevant EntityProps or AttributeProps  section.

When a Note List does not already exist, the implementation inserts the required structure at the appropriate location.

Each note record follows the internal structure expected by the erwin export format. The generated note therefore needs to follow this structure rather than simply inserting arbitrary XML text.

6. Matching PowerDesigner Objects with erwin

Once the source object codes are extracted, the utility identifies the corresponding erwin objects using a three-level matching strategy. 

Level 1 — Name + Code
PowerDesigner Name  = erwin Name
PowerDesigner Code  = erwin Physical Name

Level 2 — Code
PowerDesigner Code = erwin Physical Name

Level 3 — Name
PowerDesigner Name = erwin Name

The comparison is performed case-insensitively.

Fallback matching is accepted only when the candidate is unique, reducing the risk of assigning an object code to the wrong target object.

7. Why Byte-Level XML Modification?

Instead of reading and rewriting the entire erwin XML through a conventional DOM writer, the implementation uses the XML parser to locate the required objects and byte positions.

The new Note structures are then inserted directly into the original XML byte stream.

This helps avoid unintended changes such as:

  • line-ending normalization;
  • conversion of <X></X> into <X/>;
  • namespace declaration reordering;
  • other formatting changes introduced by XML serializers.

As a result, only the required portions of the original erwin XML are modified.

8. GitHub Repository

The complete implementation, usage instructions, and supporting files are available in the repository below.
GitHub Repository : GitHub - Writzzzz/Object_Code_Migration--SAP_PD_to_ERWIN · GitHub

The repository can be used as a reference for implementing or adapting the object-code migration approach for different PowerDesigner-to-erwin migration scenarios.

Conclusion

Preserving source metadata is an important aspect of data-model migration, particularly when the migrated model needs to remain traceable to its original source.

This approach extracts PowerDesigner object codes, identifies the corresponding erwin objects, and stores the codes as structured Notes.

By generalizing the approach across PDM, LDM, and CDM, the same mechanism can be used to retain source-object provenance across different PowerDesigner model types.

Key Benefits

  • Preserves original PowerDesigner object codes
  • Maintains source-to-target traceability
  • Preserves existing erwin Notes
  • Can be applied across PDM, LDM, and CDM scenarios
  • Supports object-level matching and reporting
  • Minimizes unnecessary changes to the original erwin XML

entry.title: 3 Challenges I Encountered When Calling SAP RPT-1.6 via the Low-Level Python SDK
entry.content:
Background

SAP RPT-1.6 is SAP's foundation model for multi-target tabular prediction: it handles classification and regression across multiple columns simultaneously, trained on relational enterprise data patterns. It is available via SAP AI Core and can be called programmatically using the official ai-api-client-sdk Python package.

The SDK abstracts authentication, REST calls, and payload handling, which sounds like it should make things straightforward. However, it introduces three silent issues that make RPT-1.6 calls fail in ways that are hard to diagnose because none of them are documented anywhere publicly. This post covers each issue, its root cause, and a way to fix them.

The environment used throughout:

  • Python 3.11
  • ai-core-sdk + ai-api-client-sdk (latest pip release at time of writing)
  • RPT-1.6 deployed on AI Core (scenario: foundation-models, executable: aicore-sap)

The prediction scenario used as example:

  • Sales order table data.
  • Prediction fields: "Sales Group", "Shipping Point", "Payment Terms", "Incoterms".
  • Prediction field placeholder: [PREDICT].

If you are starting from scratch, use RPTClient from sap-ai-sdk-gen. It handles payload construction, serialization, and response parsing correctly and avoids all three issues described below. The rest of this post applies only if you are using ai-api-client-sdk's low-level rest_client directly, for example because you were already on that package for other AI Core operations.The rest of this post applies only if you are using ai-api-client-sdk's low-level rest_client directly, for example because you were already on that package for other AI Core operations.

Bug 1: Wrong Payload Schema

Symptom

The API returns a 400 Bad Request or a validation error immediately on the first call, regardless of what data you send.

Root cause

The RPT-1.6 /predict endpoint does not accept a flat body with top-level task_type and data keys, a structure that some older SDK examples and internal docs suggest. The correct schema wraps the target column configuration inside a prediction_config object, and the row data goes under a rows key (not data).

Fix

payload = {
    "prediction_config": {
        "target_columns": [
            {
                "name": "Sales Group",
                "task_type": "classification",
                "prediction_placeholder": "[PREDICT]"
            },
            {
                "name": "Shipping Point",
                "task_type": "classification",
                "prediction_placeholder": "[PREDICT]"
            },
            {
                "name": "Payment Terms",
                "task_type": "classification",
                "prediction_placeholder": "[PREDICT]"
            },
            {
                "name": "Incoterms",
                "task_type": "classification",
                "prediction_placeholder": "[PREDICT]"
            }
        ]
    },
    "index_column": "Order ID",
    "rows": df.to_dict(orient="records")   # "rows", not "data"
}

Each entry in target_columns must have name, task_type, and prediction_placeholder. Rows that should receive a prediction carry the placeholder string in those columns; all other rows provide training context.

Bug 2: SDK Silently Camelizes the Request Body

Symptom

The API returns a 400 or 422 even with a correctly structured payload. Logging the raw outbound request body reveals that keys like prediction_config have been transformed to predictionConfig, target_columns to targetColumns, and so on.

Root cause

ai_api_client_sdk/helpers/rest_client.py, lines 86–87, runs humps.camelize() on every outbound payload before sending it. This is on by default and undocumented. RPT-1.6 expects snake_case keys throughout; camelCase keys cause a silent schema mismatch.

# Inside rest_client.py (SDK source): this runs on every POST body:
if convert_body_to_camel_case:
    body = humps.camelize(body)

Fix

The post() method accepts **kwargs that are passed through. There is an undocumented boolean parameter convert_body_to_camel_case that disables this behavior:

response = ai_core_client.rest_client.post(
    path=f"/inference/deployments/{DEPLOYMENT_ID}/predict",
    body=payload,
    headers={"AI-Resource-Group": "default"},
    convert_body_to_camel_case=False          # disables humps.camelize()
)

Without this flag, the payload is corrupted before it ever leaves the client.

Bug 3: SDK Silently Decamelizes the Response Keys

Symptom

Now we have data as the API call succeeds and returns predictions. However, when you try to extract values from the response, such as item.get("Order ID") or item.get("Sales Group"), you get None for every field.

Root cause

rest_client.py, line 117, runs humps.decamelize() on the raw response JSON. This converts the response keys from whatever the API returned to snake_case: Order ID becomes order_id, Sales Group becomes sales_group, salesGroup becomes sales_group. The transformation is lossy and silent; the SDK does not warn you that keys have been renamed.
