# Inside rest_client.py (SDK source): this runs on every response:
response_body = humps.decamelize(response_body)

Fix

When extracting predictions from the response, map your original column names to their decamelized equivalents before doing the lookup:

def to_resp_key(col: str) -> str:
    """Converts a column name to the key the SDK will have decamelized it to."""
    return col.lower().replace(" ", "_")

# Example extraction:
predicted_sales_group  = item.get(to_resp_key("Sales Group"))   # → "sales_group"
predicted_order_id     = item.get(to_resp_key("Order ID"))      # → "order_id"

This is a workaround, not a fix to the SDK behavior itself. If a future SDK version changes the decamelize step, this mapping will need revisiting. Ideally, the SDK would expose convert_response_to_snake_case=False as a symmetric flag to the request-side parameter.

Final Working Request Structure

Putting all three fixes together, a minimal working prediction call looks like this:

import pandas as pd
from ai_api_client_sdk.ai_api_v2_client import AIAPIV2Client

# --- Config ---
AI_API_URL       = "<your-api-url/v2>"
AUTH_URL         = "<your-auth-url>/oauth/token"
CLIENT_ID        = "<your-client-id>"
CLIENT_SECRET    = "<your-client-secret>"
RESOURCE_GROUP   = "default"
DEPLOYMENT_ID    = "<your-deployment-id>"
INDEX_COL        = "Order ID"
TARGET_COLS      = ["Sales Group", "Shipping Point", "Payment Terms", "Incoterms"]
PLACEHOLDER      = "[PREDICT]"

# --- Client ---
ai_core_client = AIAPIV2Client(
    base_url=AI_API_URL,
    auth_url=AUTH_URL,
    client_id=CLIENT_ID,
    client_secret=CLIENT_SECRET,
    resource_group=RESOURCE_GROUP,
)

# --- Payload (Bug 1 fix: correct schema) ---
df = pd.read_csv("dataset.csv")
payload = {
    "prediction_config": {
        "target_columns": [
            {"name": col, "task_type": "classification", "prediction_placeholder": PLACEHOLDER}
            for col in TARGET_COLS
        ]
    },
    "index_column": INDEX_COL,
    "rows": df.to_dict(orient="records"),
}

# --- Request (Bug 2 fix: disable camelization) ---
response = ai_core_client.rest_client.post(
    path=f"/inference/deployments/{DEPLOYMENT_ID}/predict",
    body=payload,
    headers={"AI-Resource-Group": RESOURCE_GROUP},
    convert_body_to_camel_case=False,
)

# --- Response parsing (Bug 3 fix: account for decamelized keys) ---
def to_resp_key(col: str) -> str:
    return col.lower().replace(" ", "_")

results = response.data.get("predictions", [])
for item in results:
    order_id = item.get(to_resp_key(INDEX_COL))
    preds = {col: item.get(to_resp_key(col)) for col in TARGET_COLS}
    print(order_id, preds)

Summary

# Issue Root cause Fix

1Wrong payload schemaRPT-1.6 uses prediction_config + rows, not task_type + dataUse the correct nested schema
2Request body camelizedrest_client.py runs humps.camelize() by defaultPass convert_body_to_camel_case=False
3Response keys decamelizedrest_client.py runs humps.decamelize() on responseMap column names with col.lower().replace(" ", "_")

 

Tested on SAP AI Core (EU Central 1, AWS), RPT-1.6, ai-api-client-sdk latest, Python 3.11.

entry.title: Preserving PowerDesigner Extended Attributes in erwin: Automating UDP Migration and Validation
entry.content:
Introduction

Data-model migration is often described in terms of entities, attributes, relationships, keys, and data types. However, enterprise data models usually contain much more than their core structural definitions.

PowerDesigner models can contain Extended Attributes that capture additional business and governance metadata such as:

Data OwnershipPersonal Data IndicatorsGovernance Properties
Data classificationBusiness-specific classificationsSource-system metadata
Design statusCreation DateLast Updated Date

When a model is migrated from SAP PowerDesigner to erwin Data Modeler, preserving this metadata becomes an important part of migration fidelity. A model may look structurally correct after migration while still losing a significant amount of business metadata. This article describes an automation approach for converting PowerDesigner Extended Attributes into erwin User-Defined Properties (UDPs), applying the values to the target model, and generating an evidence-based reconciliation report.

The Problem Statement: Structural Migration Is Not Enough

Consider a simplified PowerDesigner entity:

Customer
│
├── Customer_ID
├── Customer_Name
└── Customer_Status

From a structural perspective, migrating this entity and its attributes may appear sufficient. But the PowerDesigner model may also contain Extended Attributes such as:

Data Owner             = Customer Domain
Data Classification    = Internal
Personal Data           = No
Design Status           = Approved
Critical Data           = Yes

These properties are not necessarily represented as normal attributes or columns. They are metadata about the model objects. Therefore, a migration process that validates only: Entity, Attribute, Relationship, Data Type or Key can report a successful migration while these additional properties have been lost.

The objective of the UDP migration layer is therefore to Preserve relevant PowerDesigner Extended Attribute metadata as structured erwin UDPs and verify that the values were actually accepted by erwin.

PowerDesigner Extended Attributes vs erwin UDPs

The two modeling platforms represent custom metadata differently. At a high level:

SAP PowerDesignererwin Data Modeler
Extended AttributeUser-Defined Property (UDP)
Property name/pathUDP name
Property valueUDP value
Object identifierObject-level traceability
Extended Attribute profileUDP definition/value configuration

The migration therefore requires more than copying text from one file to another. A translation layer is required. If I try to showcase the snapshots of the transition between the two tools :

Figure 1 : Snapshot of how SAP PowerDesigner stores the Extended Attributes

Figure 2 : Snapshot of how Erwin Data Modeller stores User Defined Properties

Overall Automation Architecture

The UDP migration component was designed as a separate processing layer within the broader PowerDesigner-to-erwin migration framework. The relevant flow can be summarized as:

PowerDesigner
Extended Attribute
        │
        ▼
Extraction
        │
        ▼
Property Mapping
        │
        ▼
UDP Definition
        │
        ▼
UDP Value
        │
        ▼
erwin Data Modeler

The important design principle is that the process does not simply assume that a write operation succeeded. Instead: Write → Read Back → Compare → Report. This makes the migration auditable.

Step 1 — Extracting Extended Attributes from PowerDesigner

The first step is to parse the PowerDesigner model and identify its Extended Attributes.

Figure 3 : Extended Attributes represented in the PowerDesigner LDM XML

The extraction component reads the PowerDesigner model and builds a baseline containing information such as:

Object ID
Entity Name
Entity Code
Extended Attribute Name
Extended Attribute Value

For Example :

Object:
    Customer

Extended Attributes:
    Data Owner        → Customer Domain
    Design Status     → Approved
    Personal Data     → No

The extraction layer also creates an Extended Attribute profile. This profile records information such as:

  • Property name
  • Observed values
  • Number of distinct values
  • Coverage
  • Source property path

This gives the next stage enough information to prepare the target UDP definitions.

Step 2 — Preparing the UDP Schema

Once the Extended Attributes have been extracted, the next step is to determine what UDP definitions are required in erwin. The automation generates a UDP schema containing information such as:

Source Property:
BIM-core.DesignStatus

Target UDP:
DesignStatus

Type:
List

Observed Value:
Approved

The source property path is retained so that the migration remains traceable.

UDP Name Normalization

Source property paths may contain characters that are not appropriate for an erwin UDP name. For example:

BIM-core.DesignStatus -> can be normalized to -> DesignStatus

Similarly, characters that are not suitable for a UDP identifier are normalized. However, simply taking the last portion of a property path can create collisions. For example:

DomainA.Status 
DomainB.Status

would both produce: Status

To avoid this, the automation detects duplicate names and retains additional path information when necessary. This prevents two different source properties from unintentionally mapping to the same target UDP.

Inferring UDP Types

One of the challenges is determining the appropriate erwin UDP type from the source values. The automation uses observed values to make a conservative classification. For example:

Boolean values

If the observed values are: True or False, the property can be represented as a List containing: <True><False>

Small closed value sets

If a property has a small number of distinct values: <Approved><Draft><Deprecated>. It can be represented as a List.

Free-form values

Properties containing arbitrary text are represented as Text. The implementation intentionally avoids aggressively converting digit-looking strings into numeric values. For example: <2021.2> could represent a version rather than a numeric measurement. Treating it as a number could change the original meaning. Therefore, preserving the original value as text is safer.

Step 3 — Building the Property Manifest

After creating the UDP schema, the process creates a property manifest. The manifest effectively becomes the instruction set for the injection stage.

A simplified example looks like:

PD Object ID       : 1234-5678
Entity Name        : Customer
UDP                : DesignStatus
Source Path        : BIM-core.DesignStatus
Value              : Approved

Another record could be:

PD Object ID       : 1234-5678
Entity Name        : Customer
UDP                : DataOwner
Source Path        : BIM-core.DataOwner
Value              : Customer Domain

This separation is useful because it divides the process into two concerns:

What UDPs should exist?
        ↓
UDP Schema

What values should be applied?
        ↓
Property Manifest

Step 4 — Preparing the erwin Model

The next stage works with the erwin model. The migration utility framework can use erwin automation interfaces where available. Because erwin automation is environment-dependent, the overall migration workflow deliberately keeps the hand-off explicit. The model is prepared first, and the UDP injection stage then operates against the appropriate erwin artifact.

This is particularly important in enterprise environments where:

  • erwin may only be available on Windows
  • COM automation may be required
  • licensing may be environment-specific
  • interactive/manual hand-offs may still exist

The automation therefore does not fabricate a target model when erwin is unavailable. Instead, the workflow records the required manual action and continues when the required artifact becomes available.

Step 5 — Creating UDP Definitions in erwin

The loader performs two related tasks.

First: Create or update the UDP definitions

The process checks whether the required UDP exists for the relevant erwin owner type. For example: Entity, Model, Business Glossary etc. The UDP dictionary is then updated as required.

Second: Apply the values

Once the UDP definitions are available, the property manifest can be applied to the corresponding objects. Conceptually:

UDP Schema
     │
     ├── Create UDP
     ├── Configure Type
     └── Configure Values

Property Manifest
     │
     ├── Locate Object
     ├── Set UDP Value
     └── Read Back Value

Step 6 — Writing and Reading Back Values

A major design decision in this implementation is that a successful API call is not considered sufficient proof of migration. For every migrated property, the process records what happened.

The flow is:

Source Value
     │
     ▼
Write to erwin
     │
     ▼
Read value back
     │
     ▼
Compare
     │
     ▼
Record result

This produces statuses such as:

Applied - Verified
Applied - Value Altered
Applied - Not Verified
Skipped - Entity Not Found
Skipped - Property Rejected

This distinction is valuable during large migrations. For example:

Applied - Verified : means that the target value was successfully read back and matched the source.

Applied - Not Verified : means that the process cannot prove that the target contains the expected value. These should not be treated as equivalent.

Source-to-Target Reconciliation

The reconciliation stage joins the source manifest with the actual injection results. A simplified reconciliation table looks like this:

Entity UDPSource ValueTarget ValueStatus
CustomerDesignStatusApprovedApprovedApplied - Verified
CustomerDataOwnerCustomer DomainCustomer DomainApplied - Verified
ProductDesignStatusDraftDraftApplied - Verified
AccountDataClassificationInternalInternalApplied - Verified

This provides an object-level audit trail. The result is not merely: Migration Successful. Instead it answers :

Which property?
On which object?
What was the source value?
What did erwin contain?
Did the values match?
If not, why?

Key Benefits

  • Parses PowerDesigner Extended Attributes directly from the model XML, including source paths for traceability
  • Converts Extended Attributes into appropriately represented erwin UDPs
  • Detects potential naming collisions during UDP normalization
  • Uses conservative type inference rather than blindly converting values
  • Distinguishes real object definitions from object references during parsing
  • Maintains source-to-target object traceability
  • Writes UDP values to erwin and reads them back for verification
  • Produces an object-level source-to-target reconciliation rather than only a pass/fail result
  • Separates genuine exceptions from expected differences such as intentionally empty values
  • Generates structured Excel evidence covering definitions, values, and exceptions
  • Keeps human review in the loop for authoritative metadata definitions and environment-dependent operations
  • Provides a standalone metadata-migration and validation layer that can operate independently of the broader structural migration process

Conclusion

PowerDesigner-to-erwin migration involves more than transferring the structural definition of a data model. Extended Attributes can contain important business, governance, ownership, classification, and lifecycle information. If this metadata is not considered explicitly, a structurally correct migration can still result in information loss. By mapping PowerDesigner Extended Attributes to erwin UDPs, the migration process can preserve this additional metadata in a structured form.

PowerDesigner Extended Attributes
              ↓
          Extraction
              ↓
        UDP Preparation
              ↓
       Property Manifest
              ↓
       erwin UDP Injection
              ↓
          Read Back
              ↓
      Source/Target Compare
              ↓
       Excel Evidence Report

The key is not merely automation. It is automation with verification and evidence that is not simply to move properties from one tool to another, but to preserve their meaning, traceability, and verifiable state in the target model. That makes the approach suitable for repeatable enterprise data-model migration, where traceability, auditability, and metadata fidelity are as important as structural correctness. Thank You…

entry.title: Migrating SAP PowerDesigner Metadata to erwin Data Modeler: A Practical XML-Based Approach
entry.content:
Introduction

Data-model migration is not only about moving entities, attributes, relationships, and physical structures from one modelling platform to another. In enterprise data models, metadata such as comments, descriptions, and annotations often contains valuable business and technical context. Losing this information during migration can make the target model structurally complete but less informative and harder to understand.

As part of a PowerDesigner-to-erwin migration scenario, I needed a way to transport selected metadata from a SAP PowerDesigner Logical Data Model (.ldm) into an erwin Data Modeler XML export. The approach described in this article uses Python to read the PowerDesigner XML, match PowerDesigner objects with their corresponding erwin objects, and inject the required metadata into the erwin XML.

The solution currently implements three mappings:

SAP PowerDesigner Comment      → erwin Definition
SAP PowerDesigner Description   → erwin Note: [DESCRIPTION] ...
SAP PowerDesigner Annotation    → erwin Note: [ANNOTATION] ...

The implementation supports both entities and attributes. The major objective behind the python utility was therefore to build a focused metadata migration utility that could:

  1. Read metadata from a PowerDesigner .ldm file.
  2. Identify the corresponding entity or attribute in erwin.
  3. Transform the metadata according to the required mapping.
  4. Preserve existing erwin metadata.
  5. Avoid creating duplicate entries.

The Source System: SAP PowerDesigner

The source of the metadata is a PowerDesigner Data Model (Let, Logical Data Model.ldm).  For each entity and attribute, the script reads:

NameCodeCommentDescriptionAnnotation

Internally, these values are represented using a PDObject structure:

@dataclass
class PDObject:
    name: str
    code: str
    comment: str
    description: str
    annotation: str

The PowerDesigner reader processes entities and their EntityAttribute objects and stores them for subsequent matching.

PowerDesigner Metadata
Figure 1: Comment metadata in SAP PowerDesignerFigure 2: Description metadata in SAP PowerDesigner.Figure 3: Annotation metadata in SAP PowerDesigner.
RTF Metadata Handling

One additional consideration is that PowerDesigner can store metadata fields such as Comment, Description, and Annotation as rich-text/RTF content. The migration utility therefore performs an RTF-to-text conversion before writing the values into erwin. Conceptually, the process is:

PowerDesigner RTF -> strip_rtf() -> Readable plain text -> erwin XML

The script includes a dependency-free strip_rtf() implementation for this conversion. This ensures that formatting/control information from the source is not simply copied as raw RTF into the target metadata.

The Three Metadata Mappings

The core of the solution is the mapping layer. The three mappings are explicitly defined in the script and can also be selected independently through the command line.

Mapping 1: Comment to Definition

The first mapping transfers:

PowerDesigner Comment
        ↓
erwin Definition

The target XML structure is:

<EntityProps>
    <Name>CUSTOMER</Name>
    <Definition>Customer master information</Definition>
    ...
</EntityProps>

The same concept applies to attributes through AttributeProps. The script inserts the <Definition> element immediately after the object's <Name> element. This corresponds to the expected location in the erwin XML structure.

Important behavior

The script does not overwrite an existing Definition. Before inserting the element, it checks whether a Definition already exists. If one is present, the insertion is skipped. This helps prevent accidental replacement of existing target metadata.

Mapping 2: Description to [DEFINITION] Note

The second mapping is:

PowerDesigner Description
        ↓
[DESCRPTION] Note

The [DESCRIPTION] prefix makes the origin and purpose of the note identifiable. The script defines this prefix explicitly: DESCRIPTION_NOTE_PREFIX = "[DESCRIPTION]"

Mapping 3: Annotation to [ANNOTATION] Note

The third mapping is:

PowerDesigner Annotation
        ↓
[ANNOTATION] Note

The corresponding prefix is: ANNOTATION_NOTE_PREFIX = "[ANNOTATION]". This allows Description and Annotation notes to remain distinguishable after migration.

Viewing the Result in erwin

After migration, the corresponding metadata can be viewed in the erwin model.
Figure 4: Migrated Comment displayed as Definition in erwin. The PowerDesigner Comment is represented as an erwin Definition element.Figure 5: Migrated Description in erwin. The PowerDesigner Description is represented as a [DEFINITION] note.Figure 6: Migrated Annotation in erwin. The PowerDesigner Annotation is represented as an [ANNOTATION] note.Figure 7: Migrated metadata available in the erwin Notes section. The Note representation allows the migrated Description and Annotation to coexist with other existing notes.
Implementation Detail: From Object Matching to erwin Notes

The mapping layer determines which erwin structure receives each source value. In this implementation, the standard import often struggles with missing description and comments from SAP PowerDesigner to Erwin. The Python script steps in here to guarantee the population of metadata in the destination fields.

End-to-end processing sequence

1. Read the PowerDesigner .ldm and collect entity/attribute metadata.
2. Parse the erwin XML export and identify corresponding target objects.
3. Match source and target objects using the identifiers supported by the model.
4. Keep Comment → Definition handling separate from Note creation.
5. Convert source rich text/RTF to readable text where required.
6. Create [DESCRIPTION] and [ANNOTATION] note records.
7. Add only the required Note_List entries to Note_List_Array.
8. Write the updated XML and open it in erwin for validation.

The implementation should check the target object before inserting anything. If the relevant Definition or equivalent labelled note already exists, skip or report the duplicate according to the chosen migration policy. This makes the process safer to rerun.

Constructing the erwin Note Record

A Note is not written as an arbitrary child element containing plain text. The XML export represents each entry through a Note_List element whose payload follows erwin's delimiter-based record format. The utility builds the record fields first, escapes the payload for XML, and then places the entry inside Note_List_Array.

Illustrative Python implementation

def build_note_record(text, author, newline_mode,
                      number=1, guid=None,
                      created=None, modified=None):
    """Build one delimiter-separated erwin note record."""
    now = datetime.now().strftime(TS_FMT)
    fields = [""] * NOTE_FIELD_COUNT

    fields[IDX_NUMBER] = str(number)
    fields[IDX_CREATED] = created or now
    fields[IDX_CREATOR] = author
    fields[IDX_MODIFIED] = modified or now
    fields[IDX_MODIFIER] = author
    fields[IDX_TEXT] = encode_note_payload(text, newline_mode)
    fields[IDX_FLAG] = NOTE_FLAG_DEFAULT
    fields[IDX_GUID] = guid or (
        "{%s}" % str(uuid.uuid4()).upper()
    )

    return SEP.join(fields)


def build_note_element(record, index=0):
    return (
        '<Note_List HandleNonPrintableChar="Y" index="%d">%s</Note_List>'
        % (index, xml_escape_text(record))
    )


def build_note_array(records):
    inner = "".join(
        build_note_element(record, i)
        for i, record in enumerate(records)
    )
    return "<%s>%s</%s>" % (
        NOTE_ARRAY_TAG, inner, NOTE_ARRAY_TAG
    )

Understanding the implementation

The three functions handle different responsibilities:

  • build_note_record() assembles the individual fields of an erwin Note record, including the note number, creation and modification timestamps, creator, modifier, note text, flag, and GUID.

  • build_note_element() wraps the generated record in a Note_List XML element, applies the expected attributes, and escapes the content for XML.

  • build_note_array() combines the individual note elements into the enclosing Note_List_Array structure.

The constants and helper functions—such as NOTE_FIELD_COUNT, IDX_TEXT, SEP, NOTE_ARRAY_TAG, encode_note_payload(), and xml_escape_text()—must be defined according to the record layout verified in the target erwin XML export. The field positions, payload encoding, and GUID placement should not be inferred from a generic XML example.

Why Byte-Level XML Splicing?

One of the key implementation decisions is that the script does not simply parse the complete erwin XML and serialize it again. Instead, it uses an XML parser to locate the exact positions where changes are required, and then performs targeted modifications against the original byte stream. The reason is preservation. A normal XML round-trip can change aspects of the original file, such as:

  • Line endings
  • Empty-element representation
  • Namespace declaration formatting
  • Other serialization details

The script therefore uses Expat to identify byte offsets and then performs byte-level splicing. Content outside the modified regions remains byte-for-byte unchanged.

XML-Level View
Figure 8: XML-level representation of the migrated metadata. This provides a useful way to understand the difference between the source PowerDesigner metadata and the final erwin XML representation.

Conclusion

Preserving metadata during model migration is essential for maintaining context and traceability between the source PowerDesigner model and the target erwin model. This approach maps PowerDesigner Comments, Descriptions, and Annotations to corresponding erwin Definitions and Notes, while retaining existing metadata and minimizing changes to the original erwin XML. By using object-level matching and controlled XML updates, the approach provides a practical way to automate metadata migration while keeping the resulting erwin model traceable to its PowerDesigner source.

Key Benefits

  • Preserves PowerDesigner metadata
  • Maps Comments to erwin Definitions
  • Maps Descriptions and Annotations to structured Notes
  • Retains existing erwin Notes
  • Supports entity- and attribute-level matching
  • Provides migration statistics and optional CSV reporting
  • Protects the original erwin XML structure through byte-level updates
  • Can be integrated into broader PowerDesigner-to-erwin migration workflows

The broader lesson to convey is pretty straightforward: "A successful data-model migration should preserve not only the structure of the model, but also the metadata that explains and gives context to that structure." Thank You..

entry.title: SAP‑RPT‑TS: SAP's new Time Series Foundation Model
entry.content:
1. Introduction

SAP has released a new Time Series Foundation Model, SAP‑RPT‑TS. Its key features are:

  • Zero‑shot forecasting: pre‑trained and ready to use, no algorithm selection, no parameter tuning, no series analysis, just forecast.
  • Small, fast, and accurate: ~28M parameters, lightweight and CPU‑friendly, with strong benchmark results.
  • Relational data + covariates: supports multiple targets and past and future covariates of different data types, and provides point forecasts, quantiles, and prediction intervals.
  • Unique capabilities: multi‑target cross‑learning, horizons of up to 1024 steps, and massive multi‑series forecasting (tens of thousands of series, e.g. product × store).
  • Two ways to run: on SAP AI Core or in the SAP HANA Cloud database.

Why we built it. Time‑series forecasting is a constant need across SAP applications: demand planning, inventory optimization, financial and operational planning, and more. Traditionally, each of these use cases needs its own model, trained and maintained separately. SAP‑RPT‑TS removes that overhead: as a foundation model it forecasts zero‑shot, so a new series can be predicted without any training. It is deliberately designed for CPU execution (cost‑effective, no GPU required) and runs both inside SAP HANA Cloud and on SAP AI Core, keeping data within your boundary.

How it works. SAP‑RPT‑TS is pre‑trained on tens of terabytes of time‑series data that mirror the patterns typical of SAP business scenarios. Given historical observations and optional covariates, it returns point forecasts and prediction intervals for each forecast step. 

This blog post focuses on getting you started quickly: Section 2 presents benchmark results; Section 3 shows how to use each deployment option.

 

2. Evaluation and benchmarks

These results come from SAP’s internal evaluations on FEV-Bench and GIFT-Eval using each suite’s tasks and metrics. They have not been submitted to the official leaderboards. The notebook runs the SAP‑RPT‑TS evaluations through the SAP AI Core REST API.

Leading accuracy on FEV‑Bench. FEV‑Bench is a realistic time‑series forecasting benchmark of 100 tasks across 7 real‑world domains, with a deliberate emphasis on exogenous covariates (static, known‑dynamic, and historical‑dynamic). SAP-RPT-TS achieves the lowest mean absolute scaled error (MASE), about 1.41, and the lowest scaled quantile loss (SQL) among the models shown in Fig. 1.

Fig.1. Fev‑Bench: MASE (left) and SQL (right); lower is better

First‑tier on GIFT‑Eval. GIFT‑Eval is a general evaluation suite for zero‑shot forecasting with time‑series foundation models, spanning 23 datasets, 7 domains, and 10 sampling frequencies, and assessing univariate and multivariate forecasting across short/medium/long horizons. In Fig. 2, SAP-RPT-TS ranks near the top on MASE and continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), with a substantially smaller model than the leader.

Fig.2. GIFT‑Eval: MASE (left) and CRPS (right); lower is better

Small model, low inference latency. In this comparison, SAP-RPT-TS has the fewest parameters, about 28 million, and one of the lowest inference latencies (Figs. 3 and 4). Compared with models that run from hundreds of millions to billions of parameters and are several times slower, it reaches comparable accuracy at significantly lower cost. For enterprise forecasting over thousands of series that must be recomputed frequently, this combination of "small size + low latency + high accuracy" translates into a significant total‑cost‑of‑ownership (TCO) advantage.

Fig.3. Inference latency in seconds.

 

Fig.4. Model size, measured by parameter count

 

 

3. Getting started

The examples use a synthetic dataset with 365 daily observations for one building. The target is energy_consumption_kwh, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh). The covariates are:

  • Future covariates: temperature_c, humidity_pct, solar_irradiance_kwh_m2, wind_speed_ms, is_weekend, and is_holiday. Their values are supplied for the forecast horizon. Calendar values are known in advance; the example assumes weather values are also available. For production forecasts, supply weather forecasts available at prediction time.
  • Past covariate: occupancy_rate, supplied only for the historical period and set to NULL for the forecast horizon in the PAL input table.

We hold out the final 14 days for forecasting. In the PAL input table, their target values are set to NULL, while future covariates remain populated. Both deployment options use the same dataset; the REST request separates historical observations from future covariates. Fig. 5 shows the first three rows of the input table.

Fig.5. The first three rows of the input table

 

 

Path one: SAP HANA Cloud PAL (in‑database)

If your data is in SAP HANA Cloud, HANA Predictive Analysis Library (PAL) lets you run forecasts directly in the database.

Prerequisites: access to SAP HANA Cloud with PAL enabled. The snippets below come from the linked sample notebook. 

The model supports multiple targets, but the QRC 3/2026 PAL TSFM operator accepts one target column per call, with optional covariates. For joint forecasting of multiple targets, use the SAP AI Core REST API. PAL support is planned for QRC 4/2026.

Prepare a table with an ordering column (ID or timestamp), one target column, and optional covariate columns. Sort the observations by the ordering column, then append one row per forecast step with the target set to NULL. Each series can contain up to 8,192 historical observations, with a forecast horizon of up to 1,024 steps.

SQL example, with history and future rows supplied in one call:

-- TSFM_ENERGY_TBL: target ENERGY_CONSUMPTION_KWH is NULL for the final 14 rows.
-- Future covariates have values for all 14 forecast steps.
-- Past covariate is NULL over horizon.

DO BEGIN
  DECLARE emptyModel TABLE (id INTEGER, value NVARCHAR(5000));

  DECLARE params TABLE (
    PARAM_NAME   NVARCHAR(256),
    INT_VALUE    INTEGER,
    DOUBLE_VALUE DOUBLE,
    STRING_VALUE NVARCHAR(5000)
  );

  params = SELECT 'OUTPUT_PREDICTION_INTERVAL' AS PARAM_NAME, 1 AS INT_VALUE, NULL AS DOUBLE_VALUE, NULL AS STRING_VALUE
  FROM DUMMY
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'CONFIDENCE_LEVEL', NULL, 0.9, NULL
  FROM DUMMY
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'PIPELINE', NULL, NULL, '{"TSFM": {"args": {}, "inputs": {"data": "ROWDATA"}}}'
  FROM DUMMY;

  data = SELECT "ID", "energy_consumption_kwh", "temperature_c", "humidity_pct",
                "solar_irradiance_kwh_m2", "wind_speed_ms",
                "is_weekend", "is_holiday", "occupancy_rate"
         FROM TSFM_ENERGY_TBL
         ORDER BY "ID";

  CALL _SYS_AFL.PAL_PIPELINE_PREDICT(:data, :emptyModel, :params, result, stat);

  SELECT * FROM :result;
END;

With the Python Machine Learning Client for SAP HANA (hana-ml), run the same forecast with Pipeline.predict:

from hana_ml.algorithms.pal.pipeline import Pipeline
# SAP-RPT-TS is exposed as the TSFM pipeline operator. 
# skip_fit=True uses the pretrained model without fitting it to this dataset.
# hdf: the input table containing history and future rows with NULL targets.
# COVARIATES: all covariate columns; only future covariates have horizon values.
pipe = Pipeline(pipeline={'TSFM': {'args': {}, 'inputs': {'data': 'ROWDATA'}}})
result = pipe.predict(data=hdf, key='ID', exog=COVARIATES, skip_fit=True, output_prediction_interval=1, confidence_level=0.9)
forecast = result.collect()

Reading the result: the output table gives, for each future time point, the point forecast (forecast column), the lower/upper confidence bounds (lower/upper columns). To forecast thousands of series in one go, switch to the Massive variant (MassivePipeline / PAL_MASSIVE_PIPELINE_PREDICT), which processes them in parallel by group key.

Fig. 6 shows the 14-day forecast for IDs 352 through 365. Fig. 7 compares it with recent history and held-out actual values.

Fig.6. Result table.

 

Fig.7. Forecast plot

 

 

Path two: SAP AI Core (REST interface, as a service)

SAP‑RPT‑TS is also available through generative AI Hub in SAP AI Core under the model name sap‑rpt‑ts. Use this path when you call from an application or service, or when your data is outside SAP HANA Cloud. Send a POST request to $DEPLOYMENT_URL/predict to generate probabilistic forecasts for one or more series.

Prerequisites: in AI Core, create a deployment configuration with executableId aicore-sap and model name sap‑rpt‑ts, start the deployment, and retrieve the deployment URL. Include both an Authorization: Bearer $AUTH_TOKEN header and an AI-Resource-Group header in every request. See the SAP-RPT-TS documentation for setup instructions and the sample notebook for the complete example. 

The following is the request payload for the energy consumption example:

payload = {
    "horizon": 14,
    "data": [{
        "timestamp": hist["date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist(),
        "target":    [hist["energy_consumption_kwh"].tolist()],
        "past_covariates":   {c: hist[c].tolist() for c in COVARIATES},
        "future_covariates": {c: fut[c].tolist()  for c in FUTURE_COVARIATES},
    }],
    "options": {"confidence_interval": 0.9},
}
out = client.rest_client.post(
    path=_predict_path, body=payload, convert_body_to_camel_case=False
)

The request requires horizon and data; each item in data must include historical target values in target. The timestamp field is optional but recommended. Supply historical covariate values in past_covariates and values available over the forecast horizon in future_covariates. Set options.confidence_interval to request a prediction interval; 0.9 specifies a 90% interval.

Response (excerpt):

{
  "result": [[[528.6, 548.9, 535.9, ...]]], // [n_series][n_variates][horizon]
  "confidence_interval_output": [[[[496.98, 513.8, 503.0, ...],// [n_series][n_variates][2][horizon]
                                    [561.05, 579.4, 564.6, ...]]]],  //   index 0 = lower, 1 = upper
  "result_timestamp": [["2023-12-18", "2023-12-19", "2023-12-20", ...]],
  "detected_interval":         [{"unit": "day", "value": 1}],
  ......  
}

The response contains the following fields. The result[series][variate][step] is the point forecast; confidence_interval_output[series][variate][0 or 1][step] gives lower/upper bounds; result_timestamp holds the forecast timestamp; detected_interval is the automatically detected sampling period. 

 

4. Summary

SAP-RPT-TS delivers accurate, probabilistic forecasts out of the box, with no per-use-case training and a small, CPU‑friendly footprint. Use PAL to forecast directly in SAP HANA Cloud, or the SAP AI Core REST API to integrate forecasting into applications and services. Start with the sample notebooks, then explore covariates and forecasting across multiple series.

  2. Python Machine Learning Client for SAP HANA : TSFM Pipeline Operator
  3. SAP AI Core : SAP‑RPT‑TS
  4. Sample notebooks

entry.title: Zero-shot time series forecasting with SAP-RPT-TS in SAP HANA Cloud and SAP AI Core
entry.content:
SAP is expanding its tabular AI capabilities with updates to the SAP-RPT AI model family, which will help companies harness structured data for faster, more accurate predictions. As part of the SAP Business AI Platform, these innovations provide additional context that supports the ability of AI to reason and take appropriate action.

While large language models (LLMs) are powerful tools for handling unstructured data, they often struggle with the structured data that is critical to everyday business processes and decisions. Tabular AI is designed to handle this kind of data — it enables AI to process, understand, and make predictions using structured data found in business applications, databases, and other sources.

SAP was an early mover in tabular AI with its 2025 launch of the SAP-RPT-1 AI model and continues to bring new models and capabilities to market for AI developers, data teams, and business users.

 

Introducing SAP-RPT-TS: time series forecasting joins the SAP-RPT AI model family

Time series forecasting is now unlocked with the new SAP-RPT-TS tabular foundation model, the latest and key expansion of the SAP-RPT AI model family. Here is what makes it distinct:

  • Pretrained foundation model. SAP-RPT-TS is a Relational Pre-trained Transformer (RPT) model. This removes the need to collect training datasets, manage compute infrastructure, or endure cycles of model experimentation, tuning, monitoring, and retraining.
  • Zero-shot business forecasting. SAP-RPT-TS provides a true zero-shot forecasting experience with no model training or tuning involved. By supplying a snapshot of historical data using in-context learning, the forecast is generated on-the-fly at predict time, enabling predictions across key enterprise indicators such as demand, sales, and operational metrics. It can help answer questions like: How does demand move next month? Where is inventory projected to run short? How does revenue develop across regions going forward?
  • Probabilistic predictions. The model produces forecasts grounded in the provided context data, returning calibrated prediction intervals that quantify uncertainty out-of-the-box, not just point estimates. This reduces the risk of costly over- or under-prediction decisions.
  • Flexible and resilient data handling. SAP-RPT-TS handles a wide range of forecast scenarios: univariate and multivariate series, both past and known-future covariates, and multiple targets with and without cross-learning. It automatically manages gaps and missing values in the series, and detects seasonality, trends, and the influence of covariates to improve accuracy. Support for intermittent time series is already on the roadmap for the next model update.
  • High quality, fast and lightweight. On enterprise data, SAP-RPT-TS yields predictions that are mostly superior to state-of-the-art narrow AI forecast models built specifically for such tasks. It delivers low-latency instant forecasts from within SAP HANA Cloud or SAP AI Core, served from a cost-effective CPU environment, with no expensive GPU hardware required.

 

Consuming SAP-RPT-TS from SAP HANA Cloud

Developers and business users can immediately access the model through SAP HANA Cloud or SAP AI Core.  To use SAP-RPT-TS directly from the database, first ensure that NLP services are enabled within your HANA Cloud instance configuration, and that the instance is version 2026.28 (Q3 2026) or newer.

In the current release, SAP-RPT-TS is accessible through the TSFM operator for PAL AutoML / Pipeline models (TSFM in hana_ml 2.30). There are two ways to use it. 

  • Use the PIPELINE PREDICT function with the TSFM operator: in skip-fit mode for instant zero-shot time series forecasts:
  • Use the AutoML FIT function with the TSFM operator: which simply allows to use it alongside classic time series operators (ARIMA, BSTS, AMTSA, HGBT-TS, MLR-TS, and others) within the AutoML Time Series scenario, where it is evaluated as a candidate model and selected only when it delivers the best forecast.

 

The screenshot above captures this in practice: a PAL pipeline configured for skip-fit mode, and the resulting output showing calibrated prediction intervals returned alongside the historical series, with no training step required. What stands out is how little code is involved. A handful of lines using hana_ml is all it takes to generate a production-quality time series forecast directly from SAP HANA Cloud.

More details on consuming SAP-RPT-TS from SAP HANA Cloud can be found in the companion blog post by xinchen   SAP‑RPT‑TS SAP's new Time Series Foundation Model, incl. a sample notebook.

 

Consuming SAP-RPT-TS from SAP AI Core 

SAP-RPT-TS is also available directly through SAP AI Core via the foundation-models scenario. Getting started requires creating a configuration and then a deployment using executableId: aicore-sap and modelName: sap-rpt-ts-1.0, or latest to always reference the newest model version. From there, the model is consumed through standard REST API calls, with no infrastructure to provision and no training jobs to manage. Examples covering a range of forecasting scenarios and input structures are provided in the example payloads documentation 

.

SAP-RPT-TS in SAP Integrated Business Planning for Demand

The first SAP application to integrate SAP-RPT-TS is SAP Integrated Business Planning for Demand (or IBP, generally available in Q1 2027 release update). Planners can use SAP-RPT-TS alongside any other algorithm in statistical forecasting, running it exactly as they do today with any other algorithm and reviewing the results directly in their planning views. No new tool, no exports, no coding.

The demo above shows this experience end-to-end: a planner running SAP-RPT-TS as one of the active forecast methods in IBP, selecting it, running it, and comparing its output against other models within the same familiar interface. The integration is seamless precisely because SAP-RPT-TS fits into existing workflows rather than replacing them.

 

Try SAP-RPT-TS free

Beyond the API and SAP AI Core, SAP-RPT-TS can be explored right away through the RPT Playground, which lets you run forecasts against built-in sample datasets or upload your own files. The walkthrough below demonstrates how quickly you can move from raw historical data to a calibrated forecast, often in a single call, with no configuration overhead.
